issues.author: ClassicLarry
issues.body:
## Summary

Residual-stream (hidden_dim) scaling on the fast_track MLA + Inkling MoE stack, and the full architecture path that got there from the GQA baseline. All runs are **data-matched** (`--match data`) to the baseline token budget per rung, so the quality metric is an equal-data comparison. **Result metric: `eval/paloma/macro_loss`** (lower is better).

**Final conclusion:** at these layer depths, **2× residual-stream scaling is ~neutral on FLOP compute-efficiency (0.99–1.03×) but a positive wall-clock win (1.13–1.28×) once MFU is accounted for** — the wider matmuls run at much higher utilization (MFU roughly doubles). 3× residual is a net-FLOP loss (0.84–0.92×) but still a wall-clock win (1.10–1.33×).

Branch: [`fast_track_mla_inkling`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/fast_track_mla_inkling) @ `7cffe00c3f`
Launcher: [`experiments/grug/fast_track/launch.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/fast_track_mla_inkling/experiments/grug/fast_track/launch.py)

## Initiating prompt (verbatim)

> now lets add a variation where we scale the residual stream by 2x. then another where we scale it by 3x. for all of these, have the step count match the baseline, and have the LR match the baseline. Then do another 8 where we let the LR rescale with the new hidden_dim. flops should be relatively similar, since only a small portion of the flops are hidden_dim->kv, ->q, o->hidden_dim, and hidden_dim->latent, and hidden_dim->vocab. before kicking off these 8x2, list out the flops of these vs their baselines.

## Setup

- Ladder rungs d512 / d768 / d1024 / d1280, one 8×H100 node each, `SEQ_LEN=4096`, tokenizer `hero-bpe-v16384` (vocab 16384), MoE `MOE_TPP=60` data budget.
- Data-matched steps per rung: 2413 / 7005 / 9366 / 16839 (tokens 1.27 / 3.67 / 9.82 / 17.66 B).
- "New baseline" stack = **MLA + Inkling rel-pos bias (RoPE dropped, 128-dim content-only heads) + output latent + no shared experts + top-12 routing + Q/O latent = hidden/2, KV latent = 512 + adam-routed bias weights.**
- Residual scaling = widen `hidden_dim` by N×, **all internal module dims pinned at baseline** (heads, MLA/MoE latents, intermediate); only the residual↔module boundary projections grow. Fan-in-correct init applied.

## Path from GQA → the new baseline (Paloma macro loss)

| config | d512 | d768 | d1024 | d1280 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| GQA+RoPE baseline (`fasttrack-moe`) | 3.1559 | 2.8723 | 2.6330 | 2.5036 |
| GQA + Inkling bias | 3.1518 | 2.8593 | — | — |
| MLA + Inkling | 3.1384 | 2.8424 | 2.6104 | 2.4845 |
| MLA + Inkling + output-latent | 3.1448 | 2.8459 | 2.6183 | 2.4889 |
| MLA + olat + no-shared + top-12 | 3.1577 | 2.8571 | 2.6253 | 2.4985 |
| **new baseline (+ Q/O latent=hidden/2)** | 3.1589 | 2.8542 | 2.6246 | 2.4951 |

Takeaways: **MLA+Inkling beats GQA** (both RoPE and inkling baselines) and the gap widens with scale; dropping shared experts + top-12 + Q/O-latent compression is roughly loss-neutral vs plain MLA while buying inference/KV efficiency.

## Headline: residual-stream scaling (Paloma macro loss)

| config | d512 | d768 | d1024 | d1280 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| new baseline | 3.1589 | 2.8542 | 2.6246 | 2.4951 |
| residual ×2 | 3.1031 | 2.8173 | 2.5926 | 2.4699 |
| residual ×3 | 3.0851 | 2.8102 | 2.5846 | 2.4604 |
| **gain ×2** | **+0.056** | **+0.037** | **+0.032** | **+0.025** |
| **gain ×3** | **+0.074** | **+0.044** | **+0.040** | **+0.035** |

(LR-fixed vs LR-rescaled were interchangeable everywhere, ≤0.002 macro loss — shown: LR-rescaled.)

## FLOP efficiency vs MFU / wall-clock

Using the README MoE scaling law `L = 1.2 + 58.67·C^(−0.0842)` (L∞=1.2, α=0.0842): `baseline-needs` = compute multiple the baseline would need to match the residual's loss; `actual FLOPs` = the residual's per-token FLOP multiplier (= total, data-matched); `wall-clock` = data-eff × throughput ratio.

| rung / mult | loss gain | actual FLOPs | baseline-needs | **FLOP-eff** | tps ratio | **wall-clock** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| d512 ×2 | +0.056 | 1.39× | 1.41× | **1.02×** | 0.91× | **1.28×** |
| d512 ×3 | +0.074 | 1.77× | 1.58× | 0.89× | 0.84× | 1.33× |
| d768 ×2 | +0.037 | 1.32× | 1.31× | **0.99×** | 0.92× | **1.20×** |
| d768 ×3 | +0.044 | 1.64× | 1.38× | 0.84× | 0.85× | 1.16× |
| d1024 ×2 | +0.032 | 1.27× | 1.31× | **1.03×** | 0.93× | **1.21×** |
| d1024 ×3 | +0.040 | 1.54× | 1.40× | 0.91× | 0.85× | 1.19× |
| d1280 ×2 | +0.025 | 1.25× | 1.26× | **1.01×** | 0.90× | **1.13×** |
| d1280 ×3 | +0.035 | 1.50× | 1.38× | 0.92× | 0.79× | 1.10× |

- **×2 is FLOP-break-even at every scale (0.99–1.03×)** — the residual-width params trade against compute at the compute-optimal frontier rate. Structural, not coincidence.
- **×2 is a wall-clock win (1.13–1.28×)** because the wider residual lifts MFU sharply (e.g. d768 baseline 7.2 → ×2 11.9 → ×3 17.1).
- **×3 is net-FLOP-negative (0.84–0.92×)** (diminishing loss gains vs linear FLOP growth) but still wall-clock-positive.
- Why ×2 is only neutral (not positive) on FLOPs: the Q/O/MoE latent ports are `hidden/2` (proportional), so widening the residual doubles both the useful state and the port cost. Fixing those ports to smaller *absolute* dims would drop the FLOP multiplier and turn ×2 into a net-FLOP win — untested follow-up.

## Scale (d1280, per-token / total)

| config | hidden | active params | lm_head | tokens | train FLOPs (incl lm_head) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| baseline | 1280 | 313M | 21M | 17.7B | 35.3e18 |
| residual ×2 | 2560 | 377M | 42M | 17.7B | 44.4e18 |
| residual ×3 | 3840 | 442M | 63M | 17.7B | 53.5e18 |

## Supporting ablations

- **QK-norm** (non-parametric RMS on per-head q/k): keep it. Removing it costs ~0.003–0.02 macro loss at every rung; `qk_mult=1` does not recover. Canonical MLA omits QK-norm, but it helps here.
- **LatentMoE compression (latent/4, flop-neutral)**: "more experts, not fatter." Spending the saved FLOPs on 2× experts (768 total / top-16) beats fattening the intermediate at both scales, recovering ~half the compression penalty:
  - d512: baseline 3.1559 · 2×-experts 3.1787 · fat-experts 3.1992
  - d768: baseline 2.8723 · 2×-experts 2.8902 · fat-experts 2.9091
- **Expert gate/up init sweep** (latent experts have fan-in=latent, not hidden): optimum at the fan-in-correct value, but only ~0.0025–0.005 macro loss — a correctness fix, not a lever.
- **LR treatment** (residual LR-fixed vs rescaled): indistinguishable (≤0.002).

## Excluded / caveats

- `ink-gqa-latdiv4-exp2-d1280` is a **broken run** (loss rose vs its own d1024: 2.66 → 2.83) — excluded.
- GQA+Inkling only ran d512/d768. LatentMoE more-vs-fat and gate/up sweep only d512/d768.

## W&B runs (project `marin-community/marin_moe`)

Progression: `fasttrack-moe-{d512,d768,d1024,d1280}`, `ink-moe-{d512,d768}-re512d`, `ink-mla-{d512,d768,d1024,d1280}-re512-adam-f`, `ink-mla-olat512-{...}-re512-adam-f`, `ink-mla-olat-nosh-k12-{...}`, `ink-mla-nosh-k12-qoh2-{...}`
Residual: `ink-mla-nb-resid{2,3}x-{lrfix,lrscale}-{d512,d768,d1024,d1280}`
Ablations: `ink-mla-nb-noqknorm[-qkm1]-{...}`, `ink-gqa-latdiv4-exp2-{...}`, `ink-gqa-lat4-2xexp-{d512,d768b}`, `ink-gqa-lat4-gu{1p0,1p4,2p0,2p8,4p0}-{d512,d768}`

Run URL pattern: `https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/<run-name>`

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
The idea here was to make residual stream scaling extremely cheap (small vocab, latent projections on everything), then see if scaling it gave big boost to model quality for small change in flops. 2x scaling of the residual stream ends up being roughly flop neutral (maybe a slight boost if we retune its compute optimal ratio). The main gain here is on MFU. However the gains are not big enough to indicate its doing anything special. Basically, we just get gains proportional to the flops we spend.

What is looking reasonable is MLA + Inkling relative position bias + keeping QK-Norm (which is valid with MLA now, as seen in https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.16310). Inkling relative position bias lets us have a clean 128 dim head.

Sequence: merge #8959 (QuACK 0.6.4, the grouped-GEMM scheduler fix) and #9043 (ragged transport and fp32 weights on device back as the hero default, reverting #8884), then force a checkpoint on the live run through the training-control endpoint about 70 minutes before the cutover, mark its metadata non-temporary so the hourly temporary save does not prune it, open the launcher PR pointing `trigger_hero.sh` at it under run id `hero-ragged_a2a-ep-step<N>k`, let the old run train 200 steps past it as the paired control, cancel the old coordinator, and launch main from a pristine worktree as `IRIS_USER=marin`. Waiting for the next permanent checkpoint was rejected: step-84000 lands at ~07:00Z tomorrow and step-90000 on Thursday, and a forced checkpoint costs one step (the step-58014 precedent).

The new run carries, relative to the live one: the ragged transport with fp32 weights on device (#9043), one train-step executable per rank (#8911), the balanced ragged device kernel wheel (#8976), QuACK 0.6.4 (#8959), and the cross-entropy tile and FA4 padding fixes (#8960, #8961). The root cause of #8870 is still open; the strongest lead is a fabric fault on the racks that land at replica indices 8-10, which the trial cannot avoid.

Gate over the 200-step window against the old run on the same batches: loss within bf16 noise of the control after the ~0.006 nat dropless offset, drop fraction below 1e-3, MFU at or above the control's ~21%, no hang, retry, or watchdog. Anything short of that rolls back at once by relaunching `trigger_hero.sh` at `0908920c86`, which resumes the old run's own newest checkpoint. Runbook scripts (preflight with an NVLink counter sweep, cancel, launch, monitor, rollback) are being dry-run read-only against the cluster. A W&B report with both run sets over the trial window will be linked here before launch, along with each transition: forced checkpoint, cancel, launch, first steps, go/no-go.

comments.body:
🤖 The timing is explained by a recent code change: #8974, merged September 15 at 00:31 UTC, changed `_save_metadata` from a direct write to `atomic_rename`, introducing temporary-source deletion under the August 22 protected prefix. Both the mixture deployment (`0cb3167f39`) and nopdl deployment (`8f6f33bebe`) include it. Step 114000 was the first scheduled permanent milestone after those deployments; temporary saves use the unprotected temporary root.

🤖 Storage incident on 2026-09-23/24, now resolved. At 23:44Z the US-EAST-08A CoreWeave account reached 104.56 TiB against its 100 TiB quota, and CoreWeave suspended writes (`405 MethodNotAllowed: Account is write suspended for this availability zone`). Most of the 11.7 TiB rise since 20:26Z came from this deploy's forced checkpoints and durable handoff copies in `hero-checkpoints`.

- The step-146585 save staged at 23:43:47Z and hung: rank 0 blocked in the s3fs manifest upload, which has no timeout. Training and logs stopped with no error. The step watchdog restarted the gang at about 00:00Z (attempt 1), which restored `step-146355`.
- Russell's cleanup brought usage to about 80 TB by 00:21Z. Writes were accepted again from 00:39Z.
- Attempt 1's step-146582 save at 01:01Z then stalled. 448 of 704 processes finished their upload; the other 256, spread over 132 hosts, stopped writing at 01:01:55Z with no error, and the commit never completed. Host memory stayed about 260 GiB below the limit. The cause is not confirmed; a storage-side stall left over from the suspension is the leading explanation. Training continued because checkpoint uploads run in background threads, but the next save would have blocked on it, so the task was preempted at 01:40Z (attempt 2, again from `step-146355`).
- Since then, saves `step-146582` (02:43Z) and `step-146817` (03:44Z) committed normally, and the first evaluation at step 147000 matched the trend: dropless loss 1.9086 against 1.9098 at step 144000.
- Cost: steps 146355–146732 were trained twice, plus about two hours of hangs and restarts.
- Cleanup: about 49 TB of stale temporary checkpoints and duplicates were deleted from `hero-checkpoints`. The durable handoff copies for steps 108778, 121638, and 146139 remain. The step-81716 handoff was deleted during the incident cleanup, and no durable copy of the step-58014 handoff was found.

issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
## Overview

What is this document? This document is an attempt to formalize Marin’s policy towards what constitutes reportable, public-facing, canonical eval results for Marin models as well as the baselines we compare against.

Why do we need this document? With the first “snowball” cool-down, Marin is entering a regime where we regularly compare Marin models to existing open and closed-source models. Because Marin’s unique claim is that we are open development, we will need to hold ourselves to a high standard of transparency on how we report eval scores of Marin models and what claims we make about Marin model capabilities based on those scores.

What is in scope for this document? This document is intended to act as a living snapshot, trustworthy for any given period in time, as to the what and the how of Marin’s canonical set of evals, a set of standards to which we will aspire to hold ourselves. By "the what", we mean “which evals did we run, with what consistent set of hyperparameters and experimental constraints”. By "the how", we mean “where is the self-contained codebase that is both necessary and sufficient to reproduce our eval results independently”.

## Previous version notes

* Released Aug 4, 2026: included 11 Evalchemy benchmarks, 14 lm-eval-harness tasks, 7 Harbor agentic evals and 5 AA-II component benchmarks named as weighting targets but not run directly

## Complete eval list, with hyperparameters

### In Distribution

| Eval | Framework | Metric | Shots | Repetitions | Allowed context length | Mean time-to-complete |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | ---: | ---: |
| MATH500 | Evalchemy | accuracy | 0 | 1 run × 1 sample per item; seed 42 | 73,664 tokens | 7m 55s |
| AIME24 | Evalchemy | accuracy | 0 | 10 runs × 10 samples per item; base seeds 42–51 | 73,664 tokens | 12m 16s |
| HumanEvalPlus | Evalchemy | accuracy | 0 | 1 run × 1 sample per item; seed 42 | 73,664 tokens | 58s |
| MBPPPlus | Evalchemy | accuracy | 3 | 1 run × 1 sample per item; seed 42 | 73,664 tokens | 3m 44s |
| OlympiadBench (30-question subset) | Evalchemy | accuracy | 0 | 1 run × 10 samples per item; base seed 42 | 73,664 tokens | 1h 27m |
| MMLU-Pro | Evalchemy | accuracy | 0 | 1 run × 1 sample per item; seed 42 | 65,536 tokens | — |
| GPQA Diamond | Evalchemy | accuracy | 0 | 1 run × 3 samples per item; base seed 42 | 73,664 tokens | 28m 44s |
| CruxEval | Evalchemy | accuracy (input and output prediction, reported separately) | 1 | 1 run × 1 sample per item and direction; seed 42 | 73,664 tokens | 36m 31s |
| FinanceBench | Evalchemy | accuracy | 0 | 1 run × 1 sample per item; seed 42 | 73,664 tokens | 9m 23s |
| IFBench | Evalchemy | accuracy (strict, prompt-level) | 0 | 1 run × 1 sample per item; seed 42 | 73,664 tokens | 2m 18s |
| MRCR | Evalchemy | mean sequence similarity | 0 | 1 run × 1 sample per item; seed 42 | 73,664 tokens | 37m 35s |
| `gsm8k` | lm-eval-harness | accuracy | 0 | 1 run × 1 sample per item; seed 42 | 73,664 tokens | 5m 10s |
| `mmlu` | lm-eval-harness | accuracy | 5 | 1 run × 1 sample per item; seed 42 | 73,664 tokens | 37m 36s |
| `piqa` | lm-eval-harness | accuracy | 0 | 1 run × 1 sample per item; seed 42 | 73,664 tokens | 2m 03s |
| `winogrande` | lm-eval-harness | accuracy | 5 | 1 run × 1 sample per item; seed 42 | 73,664 tokens | 1m 48s |
| `openbookqa` | lm-eval-harness | accuracy | 0 | 1 run × 1 sample per item; seed 42 | 73,664 tokens | 1m 19s |
| `boolq` | lm-eval-harness | accuracy | 0 | 1 run × 1 sample per item; seed 42 | 73,664 tokens | 3m 41s |
| `truthfulqa_mc2` | lm-eval-harness | accuracy | 0 | 1 run × 1 sample per item; seed 42 | 73,664 tokens | 3m 28s |
| `triviaqa` | lm-eval-harness | accuracy | 5 | 1 run × 1 sample per item; seed 42 | 73,664 tokens | 31m 24s |
| SWE-bench Verified random-100 | Harbor | accuracy | 0 | 1 run × 1 agent trial per item | 32,768 input tokens | — |
| OT-TBLite | Harbor | accuracy | 0 | 1 run × 1 agent trial per item | 32,768 input tokens | — |
| Terminal-Bench 2.0 | Harbor | accuracy | 0 | 1 run × 1 agent trial per item | 32,768 input tokens | — |
| SimpleQA mini-200 | Harbor | accuracy | 0 | 1 run × 1 agent trial per item | 32,768 input tokens | — |
| DS-1000 mini-200 | Harbor | accuracy | 0 | 1 run × 1 agent trial per item | 32,768 input tokens | — |

Evalchemy ran against a server configured for 73,728 tokens. Marin reserves a 64-token transport
margin, yielding the 73,664-token evaluator allowance shown above; MMLU-Pro has a stricter
65,536-token benchmark cap. Harbor's Terminus-2 policy independently limits model input to 32,768
tokens and model output to 8,192 tokens.

`SimpleQA mini-200` and `DS-1000 mini-200` are fixed seed-42 random samples of their full
registry datasets. Harbor records the selected task names and immutable source revisions in
`simpleqa@mini-200` and `ds-1000@mini-200`; every model must use the same 200 tasks.

### Out of Distribution

* AAII 4.3

### How do we handle in-distribution and out-of-distribution evals?

#### IN-DISTRIBUTION

**We will** -- dedup against our SFT data, look at model scores while we develop the model, inspect the correlation of our ID evals with our OOD evals

**We may** -- develop synthetic RL tasks modeled on specific tasks in ID evals

**We will not** -- train on teacher rollouts from eval questions, use our ID eval instructions directly as the basis of RL data

#### OUT-OF-DISTRIBUTION

**We will** -- de-dup against our SFT raw data, look at meta-data about these evals (e.g., how big they are, general knowledge domain, etc), eval baselines on these evals

**We will not** -- look at the individual questions in the evals, look at any of our own model scores from these evals until our model is frozen, model any synthetic tasks on tasks in the evals (edited)

### Metric definitions

- **Accuracy:** the number of scored examples whose configured grader or verifier returns a correct outcome, divided by the number of scored examples. This includes exact-match rate, pass@1 with one completion, and agent-task solve rate with one trial. FinanceBench and SimpleQA mini-200 use an LLM judge; SimpleQA counts only `CORRECT` as correct, while `INCORRECT` and `NOT_ATTEMPTED` both score zero. For `piqa` and `openbookqa`, the selected answer is the option with the highest length-normalized log-likelihood (`acc_norm` in lm-eval-harness), and accuracy is the fraction of those selections that are correct. AIME24 reports the mean accuracy across its ten seeded runs.
- **CruxEval accuracy:** reported separately for input prediction and output prediction. Input prediction asks the model to reconstruct a valid function input from the code and desired output; output prediction asks it to predict the output from the code and input.
- **IFBench strict prompt-level accuracy:** the fraction of prompts for which the raw response satisfies every required constraint.
- **Mean sequence similarity:** MRCR's mean `SequenceMatcher` ratio between the response's answer span and the reference answer. A response that fails MRCR's nonce check receives zero credit.
- **Allowed context length:** This is allowed prompt + completion context length. If a model's maximum context length is less than the allowed context length, we adopt the model's maximum context length. For single-turn benchmarks, we subdivide the space into max prompt length = longest prompt in the dataset plus a bit of cushion, max response length = the remaining context window. For multi-turn benchmarks, max generation length per turn is 8192.

### Valid (Scoreable) Harbor Exceptions

For a single-step Harbor task, the following agent-terminal exceptions are valid,
scoreable outcomes when the trial also contains a completed `verifier_result`:

- `AgentTimeoutError`: the agent reached its configured execution timeout; Harbor preserves
  the work produced so far and runs the verifier.
- `ContextLengthExceededError`: the model or agent exhausted the available context; Harbor
  treats that as a classified end to the attempt and runs the verifier.
- `TurnCapExhaustedError`: the agent reached its configured turn cap without declaring
  completion; Harbor runs the verifier on the resulting state.
- `NonZeroAgentExitCodeError`: the agent process exited non-zero after potentially producing
  scoreable work; Harbor still runs the verifier. Agent-specific subclasses must be reported
  under their concrete exception type and reviewed for validity rather than silently grouped.

An exception is not sufficient evidence that a trial was scored. Include a trial in the
scoreable denominator only when `verifier_result` is present. Environment, setup, whole-trial,
artifact-collection, and verifier failures—including `AgentSetupTimeoutError`,
`EnvironmentStartTimeoutError`, `TrialTimeoutError`, `VerifierTimeoutError`,
`TrialNotScoredError`, and `VerificationNotCompletedError`—are unscored infrastructure or
harness outcomes and must be retried or reported separately. Likewise, errors such as model
authentication failures or agents killed by infrastructure are not valid model outcomes merely
because their Python classes inherit from `NonZeroAgentExitCodeError`.

## Codebase pins

| Codebase | `main` commit |
| --- | --- |
| Harbor | [`7b18505a56e5624f55887e3b20f4de452f698a7a`](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/commit/7b18505a56e5624f55887e3b20f4de452f698a7a) |
| Evalchemy | [`65c80022b8be98012a4ce6cd98a5168a7a58d99e`](https://github.com/marin-community/evalchemy/commit/65c80022b8be98012a4ce6cd98a5168a7a58d99e) |
| Marin | [`a5773eb75bda715f160cbd34e2552092cc2935e9`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/a5773eb75bda715f160cbd34e2552092cc2935e9) |

## Eval launch commands (Marin)

These commands require an Iris account with access to the `marin` controller and the `cw-rno2a`
federated cluster. `MODEL_CONFIG` must be an absolute path to a Marin model-catalog YAML file whose
model and tokenizer revisions are immutable. The model must support a 73,728-token context for MRCR.
The checkout below is the public campaign revision based on the pinned Marin `main` commit above. It
adds the Evalchemy revision that correctly applies the zero-shot MMLU-Pro policy.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/marin-community/marin.git
cd marin
git checkout ba2fef7443dd5fad1b1a35402982e1c4ce71c8c0
uv sync --all-packages

export MODEL_CONFIG=/absolute/path/to/pinned-model.yaml
export TOGETHER_API_KEY="REPLACE_WITH_TOGETHER_API_KEY"
export JUDGE_API_KEY="$TOGETHER_API_KEY"
export JUDGE_BASE_URL=https://api.together.xyz/v1
export JUDGE_MODEL=openai/gpt-oss-120b

POLICY_CONFIG_DIR=$(mktemp -d)

write_chat_config() {
  config_name=$1
  task_name=$2
  runtime_extra=$3
  max_tokens=$4
  max_length=$5
  {
    echo "tasks: [$task_name]"
    echo "task_options:"
    echo "  $task_name:"
    echo "    num_fewshot: 0"
    echo "    task_alias: $config_name"
    echo "    generation: true"
    echo "apply_chat_template: true"
    echo "batch_size: 1"
    echo "seed: 42"
    echo "max_tokens: $max_tokens"
    if [ "$max_length" != "default" ]; then
      echo "max_length: $max_length"
    fi
    echo "runtime_extras: [$runtime_extra]"
  } > "$POLICY_CONFIG_DIR/$config_name.yaml"
}

write_chat_config mmlu-pro MMLUPro mmlupro 32768 65536
write_chat_config gpqa-diamond GPQADiamond gpqadiamond 32768 default
write_chat_config cruxeval CruxEval cruxeval 2048 default
write_chat_config financebench FinanceBench financebench 4096 default
write_chat_config ifbench IFBench ifbench 1024 default
write_chat_config mrcr MRCR mrcr 4096 73728

# Deterministic single-run Evalchemy and lm-eval-harness evaluations.
uv run python -m experiments.evaluation.cli launch \
  --model-config "$MODEL_CONFIG" \
  --evals math500,humanevalplus,mbppplus,olympiadbench,gsm8k-0shot,mmlu,piqa,winogrande,openbookqa,boolq,truthfulqa,triviaqa \
  --federated_cluster cw-rno2a \
  --priority interactive \
  --version eval-policy-updated

# AIME24: ten independent launches; Evalchemy generates ten responses per question in each launch.
for seed in $(seq 42 51); do
  uv run python -m experiments.evaluation.cli launch \
    --model-config "$MODEL_CONFIG" \
    --evals aime24 \
    --seed "$seed" \
    --federated_cluster cw-rno2a \
    --priority interactive \
    --version eval-policy-updated
done

# Policy additions that are not registered as named Marin eval keys at the pinned Marin commit.
uv run python -m experiments.evaluation.cli launch \
  --model-config "$MODEL_CONFIG" \
  --evalchemy-config "$POLICY_CONFIG_DIR/mmlu-pro.yaml" \
  --evalchemy-config "$POLICY_CONFIG_DIR/gpqa-diamond.yaml" \
  --evalchemy-config "$POLICY_CONFIG_DIR/cruxeval.yaml" \
  --evalchemy-config "$POLICY_CONFIG_DIR/financebench.yaml" \
  --evalchemy-config "$POLICY_CONFIG_DIR/ifbench.yaml" \
  --evalchemy-config "$POLICY_CONFIG_DIR/mrcr.yaml" \
  --federated_cluster cw-rno2a \
  --priority interactive \
  --version eval-policy-updated

# The campaign's five Harbor policies are pinned on its public experiment branch.
for config_name in swebench-recovery ot-tblite-recovery tb2-recovery simpleqa-recovery ds-1000-local; do
  curl -fsSL \
    "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/8aa9a354d30abbda89a7756e11c1a37037aa8a65/experiments/evaluation/configs/harbor/$config_name.yaml" \
    -o "experiments/evaluation/configs/harbor/$config_name.yaml"
done

# Select the policy's deterministic seed-42 mini datasets from the pinned Harbor registry.
export HARBOR_REGISTRY_URL=https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/harbor/7b18505a56e5624f55887e3b20f4de452f698a7a/registry.json
uv run python - "$HARBOR_REGISTRY_URL" <<'PY'
import sys
from pathlib import Path

import yaml

registry_url = sys.argv[1]
config_dir = Path("experiments/evaluation/configs/harbor")
for filename, dataset_name in (
    ("simpleqa-recovery.yaml", "simpleqa"),
    ("ds-1000-local.yaml", "ds-1000"),
):
    path = config_dir / filename
    policy = yaml.safe_load(path.read_text())
    policy["datasets"] = [
        {
            "name": dataset_name,
            "version": "mini-200",
            "registry_url": registry_url,
        }
    ]
    if dataset_name == "ds-1000":
        # DS-1000's registry tasks must build their pinned Dockerfiles; no
        # published prebuilt image is available for this dataset version.
        policy.setdefault("environment", {})["force_build"] = True
    path.write_text(yaml.safe_dump(policy, sort_keys=False))
PY

uv run python -m experiments.evaluation.cli launch \
  --model-config "$MODEL_CONFIG" \
  --harbor-config experiments/evaluation/configs/harbor/swebench-recovery.yaml \
  --harbor-config experiments/evaluation/configs/harbor/ot-tblite-recovery.yaml \
  --harbor-config experiments/evaluation/configs/harbor/tb2-recovery.yaml \
  --harbor-config experiments/evaluation/configs/harbor/simpleqa-recovery.yaml \
  --harbor-config experiments/evaluation/configs/harbor/ds-1000-local.yaml \
  --federated_cluster cw-rno2a \
  --priority interactive \
  --version eval-policy-updated
```

## Eval launch commands (Standalone)

The standalone path requires an OpenAI-compatible endpoint reachable from both the local evaluator
and Daytona sandboxes. `MODEL_BASE_URL` is the API root ending in `/v1`; `MODEL_ID` must match the
model name returned by its `/models` endpoint; and `TOKENIZER_ID` must be an immutable Hugging Face
model or tokenizer revision. Evalchemy executes generated code for HumanEvalPlus and MBPPPlus.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/marin-community/evalchemy.git
cd evalchemy
git checkout 65c80022b8be98012a4ce6cd98a5168a7a58d99e
uv sync --python 3.12 --extra benchmarks --extra serve-eval

export MODEL_BASE_URL=https://example-model-endpoint.invalid/v1
export MODEL_ID="REPLACE_WITH_SERVED_MODEL_NAME"
export MODEL_API_KEY="REPLACE_WITH_MODEL_ENDPOINT_API_KEY"
export TOKENIZER_ID="REPLACE_WITH_HUGGING_FACE_TOKENIZER_ID"
export TOKENIZER_REVISION="REPLACE_WITH_IMMUTABLE_TOKENIZER_REVISION"
export TOGETHER_API_KEY="REPLACE_WITH_TOGETHER_API_KEY"
export JUDGE_API_KEY="$TOGETHER_API_KEY"
export JUDGE_BASE_URL=https://api.together.xyz/v1
export JUDGE_MODEL=openai/gpt-oss-120b

mkdir -p results/evalchemy

run_chat_eval() {
  task_name=$1
  num_fewshot=$2
  max_tokens=$3
  max_length=$4
  seed=$5
  output_name=$6
  shift 6
  uv run eval \
    --model local-chat-completions \
    --model_args "model=$MODEL_ID,base_url=${MODEL_BASE_URL%/}/chat/completions,api_key=$MODEL_API_KEY,tokenizer=$TOKENIZER_ID,revision=$TOKENIZER_REVISION,tokenizer_backend=huggingface,tokenized_requests=False,num_concurrent=32,max_retries=8,timeout=1800,max_length=$max_length" \
    --tasks "$task_name" \
    --num_fewshot "$num_fewshot" \
    --batch_size 1 \
    --seed "$seed" \
    --max_length "$max_length" \
    --max_tokens "$max_tokens" \
    --gen_kwargs "max_gen_toks=$max_tokens" \
    --apply_chat_template \
    --log_samples \
    --output_path "results/evalchemy/$output_name" \
    "$@"
}

run_completion_eval() {
  task_name=$1
  num_fewshot=$2
  max_tokens=$3
  max_length=$4
  uv run eval \
    --model local-completions \
    --model_args "model=$MODEL_ID,base_url=${MODEL_BASE_URL%/}/completions,api_key=$MODEL_API_KEY,tokenizer=$TOKENIZER_ID,revision=$TOKENIZER_REVISION,tokenizer_backend=huggingface,tokenized_requests=False,num_concurrent=32,max_retries=8,timeout=1800,max_length=$max_length" \
    --tasks "$task_name" \
    --num_fewshot "$num_fewshot" \
    --batch_size 1 \
    --seed 42 \
    --max_length "$max_length" \
    --max_tokens "$max_tokens" \
    --gen_kwargs "max_gen_toks=$max_tokens" \
    --log_samples \
    --output_path "results/evalchemy/$task_name"
}

## Standards for presenting Marin evals

* For each benchmark, plot Snowball perf, along with baseline(s) perf, on an x-y scatterplot, with y being perf and x being total training FLOPS
* Use 6ND proxy for pretraining and SFT FLOPS, and 6 * max_tokens_per_rollout / max_context_length * n_rollouts * active_params proxy for RL FLOPS
* In a separate standalone table, include all raw scores in XX.y format, with 95% confidence intervals derived from the trial count -- do not leave gaps, use table captions for results that require further context, use the exact same model family in the table as was present in the x-y scatterplot(s)
* Eval results are reportable IFF the eval in question completed with <10% of trials encountering infrastructure errors
* Eval results are reportable IFF they include provenance, in the form of model traces, and where available, verifier traces
* Any eval result that is publicly presented should clearly distinguish whether the benchmarks are in-distribution (part of the dev set), held out, or a mix of the two
* Any eval result that is publicly presented in a major release should report on *all* ID and OOD benchmarks, avoiding cherry picking, substitution, or new evals outside of a formal policy update
* For active development and internal communication, it is fine to define working subsets of the ID benchmarks and report on those in isolation

## Future considerations

* We would like to post-train multiple Snowball checkpoints, experimenting with different degrees of compute applied to post-training, to establish trade-off lines / domains
* We would like to think about a "marin model card" that would set minimum standards for true open development

comments.body: Should we plot the Pareto frontier w.r.t. inference-time compute (8K, 16K, 32K, 64K, 128K, 262K), especially for AIME? SFT on long-context checkpoints hit the 8K cap on 256/300 responses (85%), and your August SFT on 205/300 (68%). comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
👍 

I'm on board with the set of evaluations and how to run them, and I like that we'll have a policy for what we can look at. My proposal re pins:

* We define this as Marin Eval Policy v0.1
* Pins indicate the behavior now
* If we need to move the pins (to update to a new version of Iris, etc)
  - We rerun the eval suites with a representative model(s) - Qwen + Snowball
  - If the suites are identical (within noise), we update pins in place
  - If not, we need to bump the version
* Results should be reported at a particular version
* Updating the version should be infrequent but acceptable: a totally broken eval for example

I think the bulk of the value here is being transparent about all of the appropriate parameters and command lines for running we're using for the evaluations, and that we'll do our best to keep these aligned. I want us to balance the desire for replication with flexibility for making code changes, so hopefully the above tradeoff seems fair.

issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
This is the release-ready 11-model, 26-benchmark complete panel: the selected Snowball checkpoint plus ten fully scored non-Snowball baselines. - Eval policy: #9409 - Context-length ablation: #9410 - Agent-harness ablation: #9411 - Durable artifacts, exact configs, provenance, source data, and vector/PDF figures: https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/marin-eval-policy-2026-09-24 K2 is excluded because its suite is incomplete. Grug 67B A2B and the other non-release Snowball checkpoints are excluded from the release panel by the checkpoint-selection rule, but are included in the paired lineage comparison below. Step92 was selected using point estimates from this same 26-benchmark panel, so these are in-sample release-selection results, not an out-of-sample validation. ## Release-ready scores The displayed intervals follow the declared release method: scored-trial sample SEM × 1/√0.9, then ±1.96 SEM and clipping to [0, 1]. They are normal/SEM approximations conditional on scored trials, not missingness-robust binomial intervals; consequently, finite all-zero cells have zero-width bands. The 0.9 factor reflects the policy tolerance but does not correct non-random infrastructure loss. AIME24 pools repeated outer launches that did not use distinct seeds, so its band may be pseudoreplicated.

issues.title: Marin eval baselines and initial Snowball results (2026-09-24)

issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
## Overview

What is this document? This document is an attempt to formalize Marin’s policy towards what constitutes reportable, public-facing, canonical eval results for Marin models as well as the baselines we compare against.

Why do we need this document? With the first “snowball” release of a 67B A2B MoE, Marin is entering a regime where we regularly compare Marin models to existing open and closed-source models. Because Marin’s unique claim is that we are open development, we will need to hold ourselves to a high standard of transparency on how we report eval scores of Marin models and what claims we make about Marin model capabilities based on those scores.

What is in scope for this document? This document is intended to act as a living snapshot, trustworthy for any given period in time, as to the what and the how of Marin’s canonical set of evals, a set of standards to which we will aspire to hold ourselves. By "the what", we mean “which evals did we run, with what consistent set of hyperparameters and experimental constraints”. By "the how", we mean “where is the self-contained codebase that is both necessary and sufficient to reproduce our eval results independently”.

## Previous version notes

* Released Sept 16, 2026: 11 Evalchemy benchmarks, 8 lm-eval-harness tasks and 5 Harbor agentic evals in-distribution

### Details on our Evals

- **MATH-500.** OpenAI's [May 2023 process-supervision release](https://openai.com/index/improving-mathematical-reasoning-with-process-supervision/) used a 500-problem subset of the original MATH competition-math benchmark. The campaign scores one zero-shot generated solution per problem by final-answer accuracy.
- **HumanEval+.** The [May 2023 EvalPlus paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.01210) introduced expanded tests for HumanEval programs to catch incorrect code that passes sparse original tests. The campaign executes one zero-shot completion per problem against the stronger tests.
- **MBPP+.** The [November 24, 2023 EvalPlus release](https://github.com/evalplus/evalplus/releases/tag/v0.2.0) extends MBPP with additional functional tests. The campaign's pinned config is zero-shot and scores one generated program per problem.
- **OlympiadBench.** The [February 2024 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.14008) introduced bilingual, multimodal Olympiad-level math and science problems. This campaign uses Evalchemy's 30-question text subset, ten sampled solutions per question, and the configured answer judge.
- **GSM8K.** The [October 2021 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.14168) introduced grade-school math word problems requiring multi-step arithmetic. The campaign uses the zero-shot `gsm8k-0shot` completion route and scores the extracted final answer.
- **PIQA.** The [November 2019 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.11641) introduced two-choice questions about physical commonsense. The campaign selects the answer by length-normalized log-likelihood with no examples in the prompt.
- **WinoGrande.** The [July 2019 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.10641) introduced adversarial pronoun/coreference choices designed to reduce superficial cues. The campaign uses five-shot multiple-choice scoring.
- **BoolQ.** The [May 2019 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.10044) introduced naturally occurring yes/no questions paired with evidence passages. The campaign scores zero-shot choice accuracy.
- **TruthfulQA MC2.** The [September 2021 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.07958) introduced questions that elicit common misconceptions from language models. The campaign's MC2 metric sums probability mass on all true answers within each question's candidate set, rather than counting a single selected answer.
- **TriviaQA.** The [May 2017 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.03551) introduced trivia questions with independently collected evidence documents. The campaign runs five-shot answer generation and reports answer accuracy.
- **AIME24.** The [Mathematical Association of America's 2024 AIME](https://maa.org/maa-invitational-competitions/) supplies the contest problems; AIME24 is a year-specific evaluation set, not a separately introduced research benchmark. Evalchemy samples ten solutions per question through the benchmark's built-in repeat loop and scores the integer final answers. The campaign ran that 30-question, ten-repeat protocol ten times, for 3,000 generations per model. The preserved launch records have `evalchemy.seed: null`, so the outer launches were not ten distinct random seeds; every launch used the same benchmark-internal repeat seed schedule.
- **MMLU-Pro.** The [June 2024 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.01574) introduced harder, more reasoning-focused multiple-choice questions across fourteen subjects. The campaign runs zero-shot generation with a 65,536-token cap and reports micro-averaged accuracy.
- **GPQA Diamond.** The [November 2023 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.12022) introduced expert-written graduate-level science questions, including the Diamond subset. The campaign averages accuracy over three generated answers per question.
- **CRUXEval (output).** The [January 2024 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.03065) introduced input- and output-prediction tasks for short Python programs. The tracker reports the output-prediction direction, scored on one generated answer per item.
- **FinanceBench.** The [November 2023 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.11944) introduced questions grounded in public financial filings. The campaign scores one generated answer per question with its pinned LLM judge.
- **IFBench.** The [July 2025 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.02833) introduced verifiable constraints that test generalization in precise instruction following. The campaign reports strict prompt-level accuracy, requiring every constraint to hold in the raw response.
- **MRCR.** [Gemini's September 2024 report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.12640) introduced multi-round coreference resolution; [OpenAI's public MRCR release (April 2025)](https://huggingface.co/datasets/openai/mrcr) supplies the corrected multi-needle data used here. The campaign scores nonce-gated sequence similarity and selects only context-length bins that fit the served model.
- **NUPA.** The [November 2024 Number Cookbook paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.03766) introduced tests of numerical understanding and processing across representations and tasks. Existing tracker scores use the full Evalchemy protocol of 238,926 selected prompts.
- **SWE-bench Verified random-100.** OpenAI's [August 13, 2024 release](https://openai.com/index/introducing-swe-bench-verified/) introduced a human-validated subset of repository-issue repair tasks. The campaign evaluates a fixed random 100-task subset of this existing subset, with one Terminus-2 trial per issue and executable verification.
- **OpenThoughts-TBLite 2.0.** The [February 18, 2026 release](https://www.openthoughts.ai/blog/openthoughts-tblite) introduced a 100-task, faster-running terminal-agent panel calibrated against Terminal-Bench 2. The campaign runs its pinned `openthoughts-tblite@2.0` tasks with Terminus-2 and reports verifier success.
- **Terminal-Bench 2.0.** The [November 7, 2025 release](https://www.tbench.ai/news/announcement-2-0) introduced a harder, more thoroughly verified terminal-agent task set alongside Harbor. The campaign uses the pinned TB2 dataset through Harbor with one Terminus-2 trial per task.
- **DS-1000 mini-200.** The [November 2022 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.11501) introduced data-science code-generation problems spanning seven Python libraries. The campaign evaluates a fixed seed-42 200-task Harbor subset with Terminus-2, building task images from the pinned Dockerfiles.
- **BFCL-Parity @ Pi.** Berkeley's [February 2024 BFCL release](https://gorilla.cs.berkeley.edu/blogs/8_berkeley_function_calling_leaderboard.html) introduced executable function-calling evaluation. This campaign uses the Harbor `bfcl_parity@1.0` adaptation with the Pi agent, so its score is the pinned adaptation's verified solve rate rather than an unqualified BFCL leaderboard score.
- **BixBench CLI corrections @ Pi.** The [February 2025 BixBench paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.00096) introduced multi-step computational-biology analysis tasks. This campaign uses Pi on 205 `bixbench-cli-marin-corrections@3` tasks and reports binary answer-equivalence reward, which is distinct from canonical BixBench CLI v1.5.
- **τ³-bench @ Pi.** Sierra's [March 18, 2026 τ³-Bench launch](https://sierra.ai/blog/bench-advancing-agent-benchmarking-to-knowledge-and-voice) introduced knowledge and voice tracks alongside corrections to the existing airline and retail tasks. The campaign runs pinned `tau3-bench@1.0.1` in Harbor through the Pi ACP relay and scores task verification.
- **SOTOPIA-hard.** The [October 2023 SOTOPIA paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.11667) introduced interactive social-agent evaluation and identified a hard scenario subset. The campaign runs the 100 hard episodes against a fixed `openai/gpt-oss-120b` counterpart and judge, then normalizes goal achievement from 0–10 to 0–1.

### How do we handle in-distribution and out-of-distribution evals?

#### IN-DISTRIBUTION

**We will** -- dedup against our SFT data, look at model scores while we develop the model, inspect the correlation of our ID evals with our OOD evals

**We may** -- develop synthetic RL tasks modeled on specific tasks in ID evals

**We will not** -- train on teacher rollouts from eval questions, use our ID eval instructions directly as the basis of RL data

#### OUT-OF-DISTRIBUTION

**We will** -- de-dup against our SFT raw data, look at meta-data about these evals (e.g., how big they are, general knowledge domain, etc), eval baselines on these evals

**We may** -- evaluate our final models on out-of-distribution benchmarks

**We will not** -- look at the individual questions in the evals, look at any of our own model scores from these evals until our model is frozen, model any synthetic tasks on tasks in the evals (edited)

### Metric definitions

- **`accuracy`:** the fraction of scored items that pass the benchmark's configured correctness check. The common name covers executable-test success for code and agent tasks, answer correctness for generated and multiple-choice tasks, FinanceBench's `correct` judge label, and BixBench's binary answer-equivalence check. NUPA counts an item as correct only when its format-specific extraction produces a representation-sensitive exact match. PIQA chooses the option with the highest length-normalized log-likelihood before testing correctness. AIME24 first averages its ten built-in repeats per question and then averages across ten outer launches; the outer launches did not pass distinct seeds. GPQA-Diamond and OlympiadBench average their three and ten in-run repeats per question. MMLU-Pro is micro-averaged across its fourteen subjects.
- **`mc2`:** TruthfulQA's probability mass on all true answers, normalized over the question's answer set and averaged over questions. It is not a binary selection accuracy, and chance performance is above zero.
- **`accuracy (output)`:** CRUXEval output-prediction accuracy. Given a function and input, the model predicts the output; this is distinct from CRUXEval input prediction, which reconstructs an input from the function and desired output.
- **`strict prompt-level accuracy`:** the fraction of IFBench prompts for which the raw response satisfies every required constraint.
- **`mean sequence similarity`:** MRCR's mean `SequenceMatcher` ratio between the response's answer span and the reference answer. A response that fails MRCR's nonce check receives zero credit. The standard 73,728-token serving window evaluates the published bins through 65,536 tokens. After Marin's 64-token serving safety margin, the 32,768-token models use bins through 16,384 and the 65,536-token model uses bins through 32,768. Those tracker cells are footnoted because differing bin coverage is not a strictly like-for-like comparison.
- **`normalized goal achievement`:** SOTOPIA-hard's official goal-achievement score for the evaluated character, linearly normalized from `[0, 10]` to `[0, 1]` and averaged over the 100 official hard episodes. The counterpart and evaluator are fixed to `openai/gpt-oss-120b` on Together for every model.

### Other Metric Notes

- **Scale:** every metric in the suite is reported on a 0-1 scale with 1 the best and 0 the worst; there are no error counts, ranks, or unbounded scores.
- **Allowed context length:** This is allowed prompt + completion context length. If a model's maximum context length is less than the allowed context length, we adopt the model's maximum context length. For single-turn benchmarks, we subdivide the space into max prompt length = longest prompt in the dataset plus a bit of cushion, max response length = the remaining context window. For standard multi-turn benchmarks, max generation length per turn is capped at 8192. Context-ablation labels are `context window / per-turn output limit`: both values are passed explicitly, with the first applied to vLLM `max_model_len` and Pi `model_info.max_input_tokens`, and the second applied to Pi `model_info.max_output_tokens`. For example, `65k-16k` means a 65,536-token serving and Pi context window with a 16,384-token per-turn output limit.
- **Pi runtime:** Agentic Pi configs must pin `@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent` explicitly. The corrected context control pins Pi `0.87.0`; the original harness result used unpinned Pi `0.86.1`, while the first context-ablation rerun drifted to unpinned Pi `0.87.0`. Results from different Pi versions are not treated as a controlled context-only comparison.

### LLM judges

Four evals involve an LLM judge; every other eval in the suite grades programmatically
(IFBench verifies each constraint with its checker functions, MRCR uses `SequenceMatcher`,
the math evals use Minerva/SymPy, the multiple-choice evals compare selections, and the
harness/agentic evals run test suites).

- **FinanceBench:** every scored response is judged. The judge sees the question, the
  reference answers, and the candidate, and returns one label: `correct`, `incorrect`, or
  `not_attempted` (equivalent answers in substance count as correct — algebraic equivalence,
  unit conversions, rounding). Only `correct` scores.
- **BixBench CLI correction set:** every submitted answer is judged for semantic equivalence
  to the task's ideal answer and receives a binary reward. A missing answer receives zero
  without invoking the judge.
- **OlympiadBench:** Minerva/SymPy grades first, and the judge answers equivalence only for
  answers Minerva cannot establish; the reported scores come from the offline regrade, which
  uses this judge the same way (see "OlympiadBench regrade" below).
- **SOTOPIA-hard:** the official episode evaluator judges goal achievement for the evaluated
  character after each completed social interaction and returns the 0–10 score that the metric
  normalizes to 0–1.

The standard judge for all four is `openai/gpt-oss-120b` served through Together
(`JUDGE_MODEL`/`JUDGE_BASE_URL` in the launch commands; the credential is the Together API
key). Open weights and one model everywhere keep judge behavior consistent across evals and
runs, and reproducible anywhere Together (or a self-serve vLLM deployment of the same
checkpoint) is available. τ³'s LiteLLM client uses `openai/openai/gpt-oss-120b`: the first
segment selects LiteLLM's OpenAI-compatible provider and the remainder is Together's model ID.
Judge hyperparameters, per path:

- **Answer-equivalence judge** (FinanceBench, OlympiadBench): a single user message with the
  three-way rubric, `temperature=0`, request timeout 300 s with 5 transport retries, and 16
  concurrent judgments per run. `max_tokens` starts at 128 and escalates 128 → 512 → 2048
  when a completion comes back empty — a hosted reasoning model can spend a small completion
  budget on hidden reasoning and return no content — so the ladder guarantees the final label
  lands within budget. The context window is gpt-oss-120b's 131,072 tokens as served
  (Together); no truncation of the graded material happens judge-side. The raw completion is
  retained in the results for audit, alongside the parsed label.
- **BixBench verifier:** the verifier calls Chat Completions with `max_tokens=1024` and a
  structured response schema containing one boolean score. Sampling follows the endpoint's
  service defaults.
- **SOTOPIA evaluator:** the pinned SOTOPIA v0.1.5 evaluator uses the fixed judge model after
  each episode; the model under evaluation never acts as its own judge.

When a judge call fails after retries, the sample is recorded as grader infrastructure
failure (counted against the run's error tolerance) rather than silently scored zero.

### Errors and Exceptions

#### Infrastructure Error Tolerance

Modern benchmarks are prone to encountering transient infrastructure errors. Our policy is to allow a degree of tolerance for infrastructure error; up to 10% of a benchmark's tasks can be invalidated by an infrastructure failure before we invalidate the entire score for a model on the benchmark. We do not attempt to control for the particular infrastructure errors that were encountered by various models on particular tasks. For this reason, we report confidence intervals as slightly wider than they would be if all models had reported on all tasks.

#### Infrastructure vs Model Error

We categorize errors during the evaluation process as either infrastructure errors or model errors.
Model errors are scoreable and do not count toward the infrastructure-error threshold. Unless this
policy explicitly identifies an error as a model error, it is an infrastructure error.

For Harbor evals, the following error types are currently treated as score-able model errors.

- `AgentTimeoutError`: the agent reached its configured execution timeout; Harbor preserves
  the work produced so far and runs the verifier.
- `ContextLengthExceededError`: the model or agent exhausted the available context; Harbor
  treats that as a classified end to the attempt and runs the verifier.
- `TurnCapExhaustedError`: the agent reached its configured turn cap without declaring
  completion; Harbor runs the verifier on the resulting state.
- `NonZeroAgentExitCodeError`: the agent process exited non-zero after potentially producing
  scoreable work; Harbor still runs the verifier. Agent-specific subclasses must be reported
  under their concrete exception type and reviewed for validity rather than silently grouped.

For these Harbor score-able model errors, we terminate the trial and then run the verifier on the output of the agent, if any output is present. Unlike the Evalchemy timeout rule above, we do *not* automatically score Harbor model errors as 0's. This is because sometimes, agents will solve the task correctly and then get stuck in a loop of self-doubt or fail to submit properly in their harness, and we regard that outcome as closer to a success than a failure.

#### Timeout Policy

The following limits apply to every policy benchmark; there are no benchmark-specific exceptions.

| Evaluator phase | Limit | Outcome when the limit expires |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| Evalchemy trial | 30 minutes | Record `0.0` as an `AgentTimeoutError`. This is a scoreable model outcome. |
| Harbor agent setup | 6 minutes | Record `AgentSetupTimeoutError`. This is a retryable infrastructure error. |
| Harbor agent execution | 30 minutes | Record `AgentTimeoutError`, preserve the agent's work, and run the verifier. This is a scoreable model outcome. |
| Harbor verifier | 5 minutes | Record `VerifierTimeoutError`. This is a retryable infrastructure error. |

The Evalchemy limit covers the full trial, including request retries and backoff, after the trial
acquires an evaluator slot. Evalchemy [#175](https://github.com/marin-community/evalchemy/pull/175)
implements the deadline, and campaign configs set `timeout=1800`.

Harbor launch configs override task-manifest values with
`agents[].override_setup_timeout_sec: 360`, `agents[].override_timeout_sec: 1800`, and
`verifier.override_timeout_sec: 300`. `artifacts/common.sh` checks these values before submission,
so the same limits apply even when a task manifest omits its own timeout.

## Baseline Models

### How we select baseline models

The process for selecting baseline models in our policy is fundamentally heuristic and community-driven. For each new model release, we will strive to select a representative cohort of open-weights and open-source models that are roughly comparable to Marin models and document them in the policy. We will look up reported results for those models in the research literature and, where available, use them as targets for internal reproduction, noting, however, that typically the variance in hyperparameters will make published results not directly comparable to our own. We will sometimes substitute quantized variants of the listed models for the canonical models, especially for larger models where our hardware makes it challenging to run inference on the non-quantized variants.

done

run_chat_eval MBPPPlus 0 default "$MODEL_CONTEXT" 42 mbppplus false --confirm_run_unsafe_code

run_chat_eval gsm8k 0 default "$MODEL_CONTEXT" 42 gsm8k-0shot false
run_chat_eval triviaqa 5 default "$MODEL_CONTEXT" 42 triviaqa false
run_chat_eval MMLUPro 0 32768 65536 42 mmlu-pro true
run_chat_eval GPQADiamond 0 32768 "$MODEL_CONTEXT" 42 gpqa-diamond true
run_chat_eval CruxEval 0 2048 "$MODEL_CONTEXT" 42 cruxeval false
run_chat_eval FinanceBench 0 4096 "$MODEL_CONTEXT" 42 financebench false

run_completion_eval winogrande 5 256 "$MODEL_CONTEXT"

```

Run the Harbor evaluations from a separate directory so Harbor's environment does not share
Evalchemy's project environment:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/marin-community/harbor.git
cd harbor
git checkout 761fb516f6b9f05e8ff47cc3e6d91573c1496886
uv sync --all-packages

export ARTIFACTS=/absolute/path/to/eval-policy-09-17/artifacts
export MODEL_BASE_URL=https://example-model-endpoint.invalid/v1
export MODEL_ID="REPLACE_WITH_SERVED_MODEL_NAME"
export MODEL_API_KEY="REPLACE_WITH_MODEL_ENDPOINT_API_KEY"
export TOGETHER_API_KEY="REPLACE_WITH_TOGETHER_API_KEY"
export DAYTONA_API_KEY="REPLACE_WITH_DAYTONA_API_KEY"
export OPENAI_API_KEY="$TOGETHER_API_KEY"
export OPENAI_BASE_URL=https://api.together.xyz/v1
export TAU2_USER_MODEL=openai/openai/gpt-oss-120b
export TAU2_NL_ASSERTIONS_MODEL="$TAU2_USER_MODEL"

for config in swebench-recovery ot-tblite-recovery tb2-recovery ds-1000-local \
              bfclparity-pi bixbench-pi tau3-pi; do
  uv run harbor run \
    --config "$ARTIFACTS/harbor-configs/$config.yaml" \
    --model "hosted_vllm/$MODEL_ID" \
    --ak "api_base=${MODEL_BASE_URL%/}" \
    --ak 'model_info={"max_input_tokens":32768,"max_output_tokens":8192,"input_cost_per_token":0.0,"output_cost_per_token":0.0}' \
    --ae "OPENAI_API_KEY=$MODEL_API_KEY" \
    --jobs-dir "results/harbor/$config" --yes
done

# From the Harbor root, this writes datasets/sotopia-hard, the path used by the saved config.
uv run --project adapters/sotopia sotopia-harbor --split hard
uv run harbor run \
  --config "$ARTIFACTS/harbor-configs/sotopia-hard-standalone.yaml" \
  --model "hosted_vllm/$MODEL_ID" \
  --ak "api_base=${MODEL_BASE_URL%/}" \
  --ae "OPENAI_API_KEY=$MODEL_API_KEY" \
  --jobs-dir results/harbor/sotopia-hard --yes
```

## Run resumption

Resume an interrupted Harbor run only when its model, evaluator pins, runtime limit, and dataset
state are unchanged. Find the Iris root in `artifacts/config-snapshots/launches.jsonl`, then use
that snapshot's `launch.json` and copied YAML files. Replay its saved arguments with only the
affected Harbor config, retaining any `--limit` and `--records-prefix`, and add the original run ID:

```bash
uv run python -m experiments.evaluation.cli launch \
  --model-config artifacts/config-snapshots/launches/<snapshot-id>/<model-config>.yaml \
  --harbor-config artifacts/config-snapshots/launches/<snapshot-id>/<harbor-config>.yaml \
  --resume-run-id <original-run-id>
```

The durable `<records-prefix>/<original-run-id>/results/harbor_jobs/` tree must remain accessible.
Harbor preserves completed scored trials and reruns missing attempts and exceptions in its pinned
resume taxonomy. Use a clean replacement when model, policy, pins, limits, records prefix, or
dataset state changed, or when the unscored error is outside that taxonomy. Never delete a trial
directory to force recovery.

## Baseline-specific launch settings

The YAML files under `artifacts/model-configs/` are authoritative for checkpoint and tokenizer
revisions, serving context, GPU count, tensor and data parallelism, reasoning parser, tool parser,
sampling overrides, and Pi `thinking_format`. Use the matching file unchanged. Pi uses
`qwen-chat-template` for Qwen3.6 and Qwen3-Next and `chat-template` for the other models.

MRCR serves at 73,728 tokens and gives Evalchemy 73,664 after its 64-token safety margin. Ling
Lite's native 32,768-token window uses `mrcr-32k.yaml`; the historical 65,536-token Snowball
candidate uses `mrcr-65k.yaml`; every release-figure model uses `mrcr.yaml` otherwise. Evalchemy
evaluates only the published bins that fit.

K2 Horizon adds `--chat-template-content-format string` to vLLM. Its OlympiadBench, TriviaQA,
MMLU-Pro, and GPQA-Diamond runs use eight H100s, tensor parallelism 2, data parallelism 4, a 512 GiB
serve-worker memory request, and 16 concurrent Evalchemy requests. The serve settings are in
`artifacts/model-configs/IFM-K2-Horizon-MoVA-36B-A4B.yaml`; the evaluator command sets concurrency,
and the immutable launch snapshots preserve both.

## Updating codebase pins

Use the newest campaign pin for each codebase across the full release, assuming forward
compatibility with earlier score-producing runs. If a pin change causes an observed result
regression, stop launches, fix or revert the change, and issue a new policy version when the
evaluation behavior intentionally changes. Preserve the original run's exact pins in its immutable
config snapshot even after the release-wide pins advance.

## Standards for presenting Marin evals

* Select the release Snowball checkpoint by simple paired benchmark win rate among Snowball candidates. Release figures include only the selected checkpoint, not the other Snowball candidates. The Snowball candidate family includes the Grug 67B A2B checkpoint as well as checkpoints named Snowball. For each benchmark, plot the selected Snowball checkpoint and every non-Snowball baseline with an available score and total-training-FLOP estimate. Performance is on the y-axis and total training FLOPs are on a logarithmic x-axis. A baseline with an incomplete suite may appear in the scatterplots for its completed benchmarks, but it is excluded from cross-benchmark critical-difference analysis unless it has the full common benchmark panel.
* Produce uncertainty-aware normalized critical-difference diagrams with and without a FLOP control. Normalize scores within each benchmark across the complete-panel cohort. Estimate each score's task-level sample SEM from the scored trial rewards, then multiply the SEM by `1 / sqrt(0.9)` to account conservatively for the policy's 10% infrastructure-failure tolerance. With a fixed random seed, draw 100,000 score panels from independent normal sampling distributions centered on the reported scores and clipped to the metric's `[0, 1]` range. Rank models within every benchmark for each draw, using average ranks for ties, and report mean ranks with simultaneous 95% bands based on the draw-wise maximum absolute rank deviation. Report the Nemenyi critical difference at `alpha = 0.05`; it depends on the number of models and benchmarks, while score uncertainty affects the simulated rank distribution and its simultaneous bands.
* For the FLOP-controlled diagram, regress the draw's benchmark-normalized scores on `log10(total training FLOPs)` with one common linear slope, rank the within-benchmark residuals, and otherwise use the same uncertainty procedure. Treat FLOP estimates as fixed point estimates and disclose that their estimation uncertainty is not propagated. The uncontrolled diagram ranks the sampled normalized scores directly.
* We use a 6ND proxy for pretraining FLOPS, and 6 * max_tokens_per_rollout / max_context_length * n_rollouts * active_params proxy for RL FLOPS; that said, we are the only lab, as of this writing, which releases RL FLOPS, so meaningful comparisons are impossible. From the few labs who release midtraining / SFT information, we derive an unweighted mean percentage of FLOPS devoted to midtraining. We then estimate midtraining FLOPS for other labs using that mean. We estimate total FLOPS as the sum of pretraining FLOPS + (all midtraining / non-RL) FLOPS + (all RL and OPD) FLOPS. For any model which doesn't give sufficient evidence for any of the three stages, use the mean FLOPS over all models in the cohort as the estimated  FLOPS for that stage.
* In a separate standalone table, include all raw scores in XX.y format, with 95% confidence intervals derived from the trial count and the infrastructure error tolerance -- do not leave gaps, use table captions for results that require further context, use the exact same model family in the table as was present in the x-y scatterplot(s)
* Eval results are reportable IFF the eval in question completed with <10% of trials encountering infrastructure errors
* Eval results are reportable IFF they include provenance, in the form of model traces, and where available, verifier traces
* Any eval result that is publicly presented should clearly distinguish whether the benchmarks are in-distribution (part of the dev set), held out, or a mix of the two
* Any eval result that is publicly presented in a major release should report on *all* ID and OOD benchmarks, avoiding cherry picking, substitution, or new evals outside of a formal policy update
* For active development and internal communication, it is fine to define working subsets of the ID benchmarks and report on those in isolation

## Future considerations

* We would like to post-train multiple Snowball checkpoints, experimenting with different degrees of compute applied to post-training, to establish trade-off lines / domains
* We would like to think about a "marin model card" that would set minimum standards for true open development
* amd/Instella-MoE-16B-A3B-Think is not runnable currently from our pinned vLLM fork, but we would like to look at this model in the future

# Context ablation v4: context window / per-turn output limit (Pi harness)

Cohort: Qwen 3.6 35B A3B, Gemma 4 26B A4B, Nemotron Lightning 3.5. Version `context-ablation-v4`, cluster cw-rno2a,
priority interactive, rolling scheduler (cluster-wide steady-state target 20 active eval roots,
60s context-submit gap, with brief coordinated bursts allowed up to 25 roots,
and at most 3 ordinary root launches per cell). Explicit same-run recovery roots are
recorded separately when a Harbor defect is fixed. Harbor retries listed infrastructure
exceptions up to 10 times within each trial. Do not start another scheduler while
`launch-context-ablation.sh` is running; submitted roots are recorded in
`context-launches-v4.jsonl`. `QUEUED` means the live scheduler will submit the cell when
capacity opens, `RUNNING` means its Iris root is active,
`UNRESOLVED` means a successful root is awaiting record reconciliation, and `CRASHED`
means the latest root ended without a valid result after reconciliation.

Each label is `context window / per-turn output limit`. The first value is applied to
both vLLM `serve.max_model_len` and Pi `model_info.max_input_tokens`; the second is
applied to Pi `model_info.max_output_tokens`. For example, `65k-16k` means a 65,536-token
serving and Pi context window with a 16,384-token output limit. Metric: mean reward over
scored tasks, 0-1.

The first v4 validation roots used Harbor `052904f489e7307e73911a9da2b437893fe06402`; current
launches use the release-policy Harbor pin `761fb516f6b9f05e8ff47cc3e6d91573c1496886` and Pi `0.87.0`.
Both Harbor revisions contain PR #182; the current pin additionally preserves artifact-persistence
errors for policy retries, keeps DS-1000 expected-result code verifier-only (PR #199), and
classifies exhausted Daytona command polling and directory downloads as retryable infrastructure,
preserves τ³ relay infrastructure failures, makes Daytona exec-session creation idempotent,
enforces sandbox verifier deadlines, classifies compose-up throttling and τ³ target outages,
permits cross-allocation endpoint drift in resume locks, and bounds Pi's fsspec event-log
reads so timeout results can persist
(PRs #201, #203, #204, #206, #207, #208, #209, #211, #212, and #215). Pi sets
the internal compaction reserve to `max_output_tokens` and
`keepRecentTokens = (max_input_tokens - max_output_tokens) // 2`. The fixed
16,000/20,000-token compaction accounting that confounded v1 is gone.
Every cell applies the release policy's launch-level phase limits: 360 seconds for agent
setup, 1,800 seconds for agent execution, and 300 seconds for the verifier, independent
of task-manifest defaults.
Replacement launches explicitly set `retry.exclude_exceptions: []` so configured verifier
retries run. Retry execution is not an admission gate; the release policy admits results
whose observed infrastructure-loss rate is below 10%.

Runtime acceptance is confirmed on the first Gemma 65k/16k SWE-Bench root
(`/benfeuer/eval-20260922-225335-google-gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-3c8e`): vLLM reported
`max_model_len=65536`, and persisted Harbor trial configuration reported Pi
`max_input_tokens=65536` / `max_output_tokens=16384` plus resolved Harbor phase limits
of 1,800 / 300 seconds.

Model revisions: Qwen `995ad96eacd98c81ed38be0c5b274b04031597b0`; Gemma
`4d7ae4984b7db7de8f8457170b3f1a419ee76d52`; Nemotron
`a9904d24bcc1d289a1950fa9d2b978c47cf903b9`. SWE-Bench uses dataset revision
`0c553bd6d05d451907afb8db31dba84759ccc993`; Terminal-Bench uses
`693231ec029249e7c91ed2e414bcc9c45d7cd879`. Runnable inputs live in
`model-configs/ctxablation-v4/` and `harbor-configs/ctxablation-v4-*.yaml`.
The invalid v1 and v2 trackers are preserved as dated deprecated copies.

## Terminal-Bench 2
