comments.body:
# Training FLOPs Analysis: Trinity Large, Nemotron 3 Super, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, Gemma 4 31B (+ vanilla MLA models)
 
Per-token **forward-pass** FLOPs, decomposed into sequence-length-independent attention projections, MLP/MoE, and the quadratic (context-dependent) attention term. Multiply by 3× for training (fwd + bwd). Embedding/LM-head FLOPs excluded from the breakdown tables (~+4–5% on totals). Quadratic terms use causal averaging and honor each model's sliding windows, compression ratios, and top-k caps.
 
## 1. Architecture comparison
 
| | Trinity Large | Nemotron 3 Super | DeepSeek-V4-Flash | Gemma 4 31B |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Total / active params | 400B / 13B | 120.6B / 12.7B | 284B / 13B | ~30.7B dense |
| Layers | 60 (first 6 dense FFN) | 88 (≈40 Mamba-2 + 40 LatentMoE + 8 attention¹) | 43, all-MoE | 60 |
| d_model | 3,072 | 4,096 | 4,096 | ~5,120¹ |
| Attention | 3:1 local:global GQA (48Q/8KV, dh=128), SWA window 4096 local w/ RoPE, NoPE global, gated attention | GQA global anchors only (32Q/2KV, dh=128), NoPE; Mamba-2 carries most sequence mixing | 2 SWA layers, then interleaved CSA (4:1 compression + top-512 sparse via lightning indexer + 128-tok window) and HCA (128:1 compression, dense); MQA 64 heads × dim 512, shared K=V | 5:1 local:global; local = GQA 32Q/16KV dh=256, window 1024; global = 32Q/4KV dh=512, unified K=V, p-RoPE |
| FFN | MoE: 1 shared + 256 routed (expert 3072), top-4 | LatentMoE: routing in 1024-dim latent, 512 experts (hidden 2688), top-22 + shared (5376), relu² | 1 shared + 256 routed (hidden 2048), top-6; hash routing first 3 layers | Dense SwiGLU, ~21.5k intermediate¹ |
| Pretraining tokens | 17T (+ ~117B ctx extension @ 256K) | 25T | 32T | undisclosed (~15T assumed) |
| Pretrain seq / max context | 8,192 / 256–512K | 8K-class (assumed) / 1M | 8K (assumed) / 1M native | 32K (assumed) / 256K |
 
¹ Estimated: Nemotron's 40/40/8 layer split exactly reproduces the published 12.7B active and 120.6B total parameter counts. Gemma 4 31B's hidden/FFN dims are inferred (d=5120, I=21504 reproduces ~30.7B given the published head config).
 
## 2. Sequence-length scaling: all models at a glance
 
**Total forward FLOPs per token** (multiply by 3× for training):
 
| Model | 8K | 32K | 128K | 256K | 1M |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Trinity Large | 29.2G | 34.6G | 52.9G | 77.1G | 222.1G |
| Nemotron 3 Super | 24.2G | 25.8G | 32.2G | 40.8G | 92.4G |
| DeepSeek-V4-Flash | 28.1G | 29.4G | 34.6G | 41.6G | 83.5G |
| Gemma 4 31B | 60.0G | 68.2G | 100.4G | 143.4G | 401.1G¹ |
| DeepSeek-V3 (MLA) | 91.9G | 153.3G | 398.9G | 726.4G | 2.69T¹ |
| Kimi K2 (MLA) | 71.3G | 102.0G | 224.8G | 388.5G | 1.37T¹ |
| Moonlight-16B (MLA) | 5.6G | 9.0G | 22.6G | 40.7G | 149.4G¹ |
 
**Quadratic-attention share of per-token compute:**
 
| Model | 8K | 32K | 128K | 256K | 1M |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Trinity Large | 17% | 30% | 54% | 68% | 89% |
| Nemotron 3 Super | 2% | 8% | 27% | 42% | 74% |
| DeepSeek-V4-Flash | 9% | 13% | 26% | 39% | 69% |
| Gemma 4 31B | 7% | 18% | 44% | 61% | 86% |
| DeepSeek-V3 (MLA) | 22% | 53% | 82% | 90% | 97% |
| Kimi K2 (MLA) | 14% | 40% | 73% | 84% | 96% |
| Moonlight-16B (MLA) | 20% | 50% | 80% | 89% | 97% |
 
¹ Extrapolated beyond the model's supported/native context (Gemma caps at 256K; DeepSeek-V3 at 128K; Kimi K2 at 128–256K) — shown to illustrate architectural scaling.
 
Takeaways: vanilla MLA scales worst with length (full quadratic attention in every layer, head-rich by design — DeepSeek-V3 pays 81,920 FLOPs per token-key-layer vs. 24,576 for a Trinity global layer); windowed-hybrid models (Trinity, Gemma) defer but don't escape the quadratic wall via their global layers; Nemotron and V4-Flash flatten the curve structurally — Nemotron by having almost no attention layers (paying a flat ~9G/token Mamba cost instead), V4-Flash by capping CSA at top-512 compressed entries so only the FP4 indexer and 128:1-compressed HCA layers grow with S.
 
## 3. Per-token FLOPs by component and sequence length (detail)
 
### Trinity Large — 45 local layers (w=4096), 15 global
 
| Seq len | ATTN proj | MLP/MoE | Quadratic | Total | Quad share |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8K | 7.6G | 16.7G | 4.9G | 29.2G | 17% |
| 32K | 7.6G | 16.7G | 10.3G | 34.6G | 30% |
| 128K | 7.6G | 16.7G | 28.6G | 52.9G | 54% |
| 256K | 7.6G | 16.7G | 52.8G | 77.1G | 68% |
| 1M | 7.6G | 16.7G | 197.8G | 222.1G | 89% |
 
### Nemotron 3 Super — ~8 attention layers; Mamba-2 shown separately (flat in S)
 
| Seq len | ATTN proj | LatentMoE | Quadratic | Mamba-2 | Total | Quad share |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8K | 0.57G | 14.1G | 0.54G | 9.0G | 24.2G | 2% |
| 32K | 0.57G | 14.1G | 2.1G | 9.0G | 25.8G | 8% |
| 128K | 0.57G | 14.1G | 8.6G | 9.0G | 32.2G | 27% |
| 256K | 0.57G | 14.1G | 17.2G | 9.0G | 40.8G | 42% |
| 1M | 0.57G | 14.1G | 68.7G | 9.0G | 92.4G | 74% |
 
### DeepSeek-V4-Flash — CSA quadratic saturates (top-512 + 128 window); only the FP4 indexer and 128:1-compressed HCA grow with S
 
| Seq len | ATTN proj | MoE | Quadratic | Total | Quad share |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8K | 10.3G | 15.2G | 2.6G | 28.1G | 9% |
| 32K | 10.3G | 15.2G | 3.9G | 29.4G | 13% |
| 128K | 10.3G | 15.2G | 9.1G | 34.6G | 26% |
| 256K | 10.3G | 15.2G | 16.1G | 41.6G | 39% |
| 1M | 10.3G | 15.2G | 58.0G | 83.5G | 69% |
 
### Gemma 4 31B — 50 local (w=1024) + 10 global (32 heads at dh=512 on the global layers)
 
| Seq len | ATTN proj | MLP | Quadratic | Total | Quad share |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8K | 16.2G | 39.6G | 4.3G | 60.0G | 7% |
| 32K | 16.2G | 39.6G | 12.4G | 68.2G | 18% |
| 128K | 16.2G | 39.6G | 44.6G | 100.4G | 44% |
| 256K | 16.2G | 39.6G | 87.6G | 143.4G | 61% |
| 1M² | 16.2G | 39.6G | 345.3G | 401.1G | 86% |
 
² Hypothetical; Gemma 4 caps at 256K.
 
## 4. Vanilla Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) models
 
Vanilla = DeepSeek-V2/V3-style MLA, full attention every layer, no sparse indexer or hybrid: **DeepSeek-V2/V2.5/V3/R1/V3.1, Kimi K2/K2.5/K2.6, Moonlight-16B-A3B, LongCat-Flash series, Sarvam 105B.** Not vanilla: DeepSeek-V3.2 (MLA+DSA), GLM-5 (MLA+DSA), Ling 2.5 (MLA + linear hybrid).
 
MLA quadratic term (training-time, materialized K/V): 2 × n_heads × (d_qk + d_v) = 2 × n_heads × 320 FLOPs per token-key-layer; every layer global.
 
### DeepSeek-V3 / R1 — 61 layers, 128 heads, 37B active, 14.8T tokens @ 4K
 
| Seq len | ATTN proj | MoE | Quadratic | Total | Quad share |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8K | 22.8G | 48.6G | 20.5G | 91.9G | 22% |
| 32K | 22.8G | 48.6G | 81.9G | 153.3G | 53% |
| 128K | 22.8G | 48.6G | 327.5G | 398.9G | 82% |
| 256K | 22.8G | 48.6G | 655.0G | 726.4G | 90% |
| 1M | 22.8G | 48.6G | 2.62T | 2.69T | 97% |
 
### Kimi K2 — 61 layers, 64 heads, 32B active, 15.5T tokens @ 4K
 
| Seq len | ATTN proj | MoE | Quadratic | Total | Quad share |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8K | 12.3G | 48.7G | 10.2G | 71.3G | 14% |
| 32K | 12.3G | 48.7G | 40.9G | 102.0G | 40% |
| 128K | 12.3G | 48.7G | 163.7G | 224.8G | 73% |
| 256K | 12.3G | 48.7G | 327.5G | 388.5G | 84% |
| 1M | 12.3G | 48.7G | 1.31T | 1.37T | 96% |
 
### Moonlight-16B-A3B — 27 layers, 16 heads (no q-compression), ~3B active, 5.7T tokens
 
| Seq len | ATTN proj | MoE | Quadratic | Total | Quad share |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8K | 0.74G | 3.7G | 1.1G | 5.6G | 20% |
| 32K | 0.74G | 3.7G | 4.5G | 9.0G | 50% |
| 128K | 0.74G | 3.7G | 18.1G | 22.6G | 80% |
| 256K | 0.74G | 3.7G | 36.2G | 40.7G | 89% |
| 1M | 0.74G | 3.7G | 145.0G | 149.4G | 97% |
 
## 5. Total training compute (3 × per-token fwd × tokens, at native pretrain length)
 
| Model | Tokens | Per-token fwd | Training FLOPs |
|---|---|---|---|
| Trinity Large | 17T @ 8K + 117B @ 256K | 29.2G / 77.1G | ~1.5e24 (ctx extension ≈ +1.8%) |
| Nemotron 3 Super | 25T @ 8K | 24.2G | ~1.8e24 |
| DeepSeek-V4-Flash | 32T @ 8K | 28.1G | ~2.7e24 |
| Gemma 4 31B | ~15T (assumed) @ 32K (assumed) | 68.2G | ~3.1e24 |
| DeepSeek-V3 | 14.8T @ 4K | 81.6G | ~3.6e24 |
| Kimi K2 | 15.5T @ 4K | 66.1G | ~3.1e24 |
| Moonlight-16B-A3B | 5.7T @ 8K | 5.6G | ~9.6e22 |
 
Add ~4–5% for embeddings/LM head, plus a few percent for MTP heads where applicable (Nemotron: 2 shared-weight MTP layers; DeepSeek V4/V3: MTP depth 1).
 
## 6. Key observations
 
- **Active-parameter parity equalizes short-context cost.** The ~13B-active sparse models (Trinity, Nemotron, V4-Flash) all land at ~24–29 GFLOPs/token at 8K despite 120B–400B total params. Dense Gemma 31B costs ~2.4× as much per token as models with far more capacity.
- **Long-context divergence is entirely in the quadratic term.** At 1M tokens per token: Gemma (hypothetical) 401G, Trinity 222G, Nemotron 92G, V4-Flash 84G — vs. vanilla-MLA DeepSeek-V3 at 2.69T.
- **MLA compresses the KV cache, not the compute.** Training-time quadratic cost per key is *higher* than GQA (DeepSeek-V3: 81,920 FLOPs/token-key-layer vs. 24,576 for a Trinity global layer), and every layer is global. At 128K, DeepSeek-V3 is 82% quadratic — the V3 → V3.2 (DSA) → V4 (CSA/HCA) progression is this table being fixed release by release (~45× quadratic reduction at 1M).
- **Kimi K2's head cut (128→64) is a pure compute knob** — halves the quadratic term and most attention projections while keeping the same latent cache.
- **Sliding windows shift the crossover, not the asymptote**: Trinity (3:1, w=4096) and Gemma (5:1, w=1024) still become global-layer-dominated by ~128K. Gemma's global layers are expensive per key (dh=512 on both QK and AV).
- **Nemotron pays a flat ~9 GFLOPs/token Mamba tax at every length** instead of a growing attention bill; DeepSeek V4's CSA core attention is constant in S by construction.
- **Trinity's 256K context extension cost <2% of the run** because the 45 local layers stayed windowed at 4096.
## 7. Assumptions & caveats
 
- Training multiplier 3× forward (standard fwd+bwd); "6ND + ε" holds for all models.
- Nemotron 3 Super: 8-attention-layer count and 8K pretrain length inferred (former validated against published parameter counts). Mamba-2 scan FLOPs approximated (~small vs. projections).
- DeepSeek-V4-Flash: pretrain seq assumed 8K (quadratic term barely moves 4K–32K, so totals are robust); SWA-branch KV projections approximated pending the open-source reference implementation.
- Gemma 4 31B: hidden/FFN dims, token count, and pretrain length estimated (undisclosed).
- Trinity used intra-document attention masking, which shaves its effective quadratic term below the causal-average figures shown.
- Moonlight config assumed to follow DeepSeek-V2-Lite dims (d=2048, 27 layers, 16 heads, kv_lora=512, 64 experts top-6 + 2 shared @ 1408).
### Sources

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body: If we were to run at 4k seqlen for most of the training run, the training flop overhead from MLA is 20% for full MLA on every layer, and 5% if we only use on 1/4th of the layers. For a 4x KV cache reduction + leaving the door open to introduce a lightning indexer during midtraining, this tradeoff doesn't seem that bad. I think we could go either way on it here, and the biggest factor will be how the training tokens per second plays out on our hardware.

comments.body:
Mentioned by @ClassicLarry at https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/5151#issuecomment-4336418404 as a direction to explore, and again [on Discord](https://discord.com/channels/1354881461060243556/1516857141514997881) in relation to the GLM-5.2 release.

There was also a brief discussion of MLA in 2025 [on Discord](https://discord.com/channels/1354881461060243556/1380235124011958313/1397673126854267012), summarized by Claude:
  - What MLA buys you: willheld — "for MLA, the inference benefit is mostly in RAM… because you 
  don't need to save the KV cache, just the latent cache." The win is serving memory, not loss.
  - The RoPE incompatibility (the central design wrinkle for your issue): "RoPE would mean you 
  need to materialize the full K vectors and therefore make MLA bad. So DeepSeek and Kimi folks 
  do just a tiny bit of RoPE to add some positional signal with a smaller perf cost." (msg
  (https://discord.com/channels/1354881461060243556/1380235124011958313/1397673126854267012)) —
  i.e. the decoupled/partial-RoPE trick. He pointed at Jianlin Su's kexue.fm
  (https://kexue.fm/archives/10862) (the RoPE author, now at Kimi), and a follow-up post
  (https://kexue.fm/archives/11111) arguing partial RoPE should be theoretically better.
  - The evaluation problem (flagged by dlwh, still unresolved): "we need to figure out how to 
  evaluate these inference-time things. KV reuse, MLA, GQA, alternating SWA… we want to know the
  bpb hit, and inference time/space can be its own measurement." willheld concurred the
  partial-RoPE effect is "not too likely to show up in C4 loss" — so a fair MLA eval needs
  long-context signal plus a separate inference time/space measurement, not just BPB.
  - willheld said he "planned to run MLA" after his then-current work — but no run ever surfaces
  in the corpus, so this didn't land.

spillover_issues.author: dlwh
spillover_issues.body:
## Description
Expand `experiments/evals/ppl_circuit_coverage_v2.py` with small, reviewable circuit/task families for issue #6070. These probes should test basic code-interpretation functionality with compact few-shot ICL, target-only supervised validation, and plain-text training documents.

Workflow for a contributor:

1. Pick one small task or family.
2. Add a `PplCircuitCoverageV2Family` value if needed, add slices to `PPL_CIRCUIT_COVERAGE_V2_SLICES`, implement `_generate_<task>`, and register it in `_GENERATORS`.
3. Keep prompts compact: completed few-shot lines followed by one completion prefix. Do not add `Family:`, `Task:`, `Prompt:`, `worked examples`, `held-out query`, `answer:`, or `Final answer:`.
4. Return supervised rows with `input` ending before the held-out answer and `output` containing only the final answer plus newline.
5. Generate a small local sample:
   `uv run python -c 'from experiments.evals.ppl_circuit_coverage_v2 import write_local_sample; write_local_sample("/tmp/ppl_circuit_v2_sample", examples_per_config=36)'`
6. Inspect the plain-text ICL examples manually for ambiguity, leakage, and broken escaping.
7. Run validation tests:
   `uv run --with pytest --with pytest-timeout pytest -m "not slow" tests/evals/test_ppl_circuit_coverage_v2.py -q`
8. Confirm the plain-text training renderer still produces `input + output`, and that the raw validation split uses supervised `input`/`output` target-only scoring.

Good first task candidates:

- String parsing: split/join, prefix/suffix trimming, delimiter extraction, balanced quote parsing.
- Structured data: JSONPath-lite lookup, nested Python literal lookup, CSV quoting/escaping.
- Arithmetic: integer division/remainder, bitwise ops, small rational simplification, date arithmetic.
- Code semantics: boolean expression evaluation, operator precedence, small loop trace, function-call argument binding.
- Text formatting: indentation normalization, bullet renumbering, fixed-width alignment.
- State machines: URL/path normalization, simple lexer tokenization, calculator stack traces.

### Definition of Done
- One new task or tightly related family is added to the v2 generator and registry.
- Generated local samples include at least 36 examples for the new task and look correct on manual inspection.
- Tests verify the target from metadata and enforce compact target-only supervised formatting.
- The PR includes five representative generated examples in the description.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 # Research

The file the issue asks to expand (`experiments/evals/ppl_circuit_coverage_v2.py`) doesn't exist on `main`; it lives only on branch `codex/ppl-circuit-v2`, in flight as PR #6207 ([`Add PPL circuit coverage v2 generators`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/6207)). Any new task-family work must either land after #6207 merges or stack on its branch (which will conflict on the registry tuple and `_GENERATORS` dict).

The existing six families cover string/byte transforms, indexing, arithmetic, structured serialization, state machines, and format/style. The issue's "Code semantics" candidates — boolean expression evaluation, operator precedence, small loop trace, function-call argument binding — are not yet covered by any family.

**Relevant code (from PR #6207's branch)**
- [`ppl_circuit_coverage_v2.py#L40-L47`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/codex/ppl-circuit-v2/experiments/evals/ppl_circuit_coverage_v2.py#L40-L47) — `PplCircuitCoverageV2Family` enum
- [`ppl_circuit_coverage_v2.py#L87-L114`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/codex/ppl-circuit-v2/experiments/evals/ppl_circuit_coverage_v2.py#L87-L114) — `PPL_CIRCUIT_COVERAGE_V2_SLICES` registry
- [`ppl_circuit_coverage_v2.py#L1224-L1252`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/codex/ppl-circuit-v2/experiments/evals/ppl_circuit_coverage_v2.py#L1224-L1252) — `_GENERATORS` dispatch
- [`ppl_circuit_coverage_v2.py#L220-L244`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/codex/ppl-circuit-v2/experiments/evals/ppl_circuit_coverage_v2.py#L220-L244) — `_generate_string_slicing` pattern to follow
- [`ppl_circuit_coverage_v2.py#L1329-L1342`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/codex/ppl-circuit-v2/experiments/evals/ppl_circuit_coverage_v2.py#L1329-L1342) — `_pretraining_weight` must learn the new family

# Proposed Fix

Add a `CODE_SEMANTICS` family targeting the one gap suggested by the issue. Three task generators, each ~50 lines plus shared helpers and tests — total expected diff ~350-450 lines plus five generated example snippets in the PR body, which exceeds the 100-line auto-PR threshold and is a new feature, so I am holding for review rather than pushing.

Proposed slices:
1. `bool_expr_eval` — short Python-like boolean expression over named ints/bools (`(a < b) and not c` with `a=2, b=5, c=False`), target is the literal `True`/`False`.
2. `operator_precedence` — small integer arithmetic with mixed `+ - * / // % **`, target is the integer/float result Python would produce.
3. `function_arg_binding` — given `def f(a, b=2, *, c): ...` and a call like `f(1, c=7)`, target is the bound `{"a":1,"b":2,"c":7}` dict.

Each generator follows the existing recipe: two completed few-shot lines via `_few_shot_block`, one completion prefix terminated by ` -> `, target wrapped via `_record(...)` with operation/text metadata. Plain-text weight 2 in `_pretraining_weight` (parity with `ARITHMETIC` / `STRUCTURED_SERIALIZATION`).

Tests mirror the existing pattern: extend `test_ppl_circuit_coverage_v2_slices_include_basic_functionality_families` (or add a `code_semantics` analogue), add a `test_code_semantics_targets_match_metadata` that recomputes each target from `metadata`, and add the family to the leak/format assertion set.

**Blockers / questions before I start:**
- This stacks on PR #6207. Should I (a) wait for #6207 to land then PR against `main`, or (b) branch from `codex/ppl-circuit-v2` and open a follow-up PR against `main` that will rebase after #6207 merges?
- Confirm `CODE_SEMANTICS` is the desired gap. The other uncovered candidate from the issue is structured-data lookup (JSONPath-lite / nested-literal lookup) which would extend `STRUCTURED_SERIALIZATION` instead of a new family.

Holding implementation until one of those is confirmed.

comments.author: dlwh
comments.body:
🤖 Forward/backward profile handoff for the current Grug MoE D2560 CoreWeave work.

Context:

- We pivoted from MuonH optimizer work back to the non-optimizer train step because the best single-node SGD profile is still only around `16 MFU`.
- Current clean reference is the May141 single-node SGD profile:
  - Run: `GM2560-MAY-141S4096-W2048-B8-R1-E8M1-XLACE-RING-REPEMB-REPOUT-FA4SGD-AUTOTUNE-PROFILE-N1-cw-20260618-0637`
  - Shape: 1 H100 node, batch `8`, seq_len `4096`, sliding_window `2048`, `replica=1`, `expert=8`, `model=1`
  - Attention: `gpu_fa4_cute`
  - CE: XLA CE
  - MoE: ring
  - Optimizer: SGD, so this is mostly fwd+bwd without MuonH dominating
  - Result: `16.1876 MFU`, `74848.2 tokens/s`, `0.4378s/step`
  - Local profile copy was downloaded to `scratch/profiles/may141` and served during the investigation on port `6009`.

What is already fixed / likely not the primary bottleneck:

- FA4 had an earlier pathological batch all-gather before the attention FFI. The fix was to force the FA4 CuTe FFI through a batch-axis `shard_map` so XLA does not implicitly all-gather the batch argument. That made the accidental attention collective go away.
- After that fix, attention is no longer the obvious dominant explanation for 16 MFU. It still needs normal accounting, but the earlier dumb FA4 all-gather is not the current suspected bottleneck.
- Tensor parallelism is intentionally out of scope here. Keep `model_axis=1` for these runs.

Current uncertainty:

- The MoE block is likely a major part of the remaining step time, but we have not cleanly separated **expert matmul/GMM compute** from **router/permute/unpermute/gather-scatter layout work**.
- The profile labels are still too coarse in the relevant region. Seeing `gemm_fusion_dot` / NVJIT-like kernels near the MoE region does not prove the expert matmuls are the bottleneck; those kernels may be adjacent to, or interleaved with, routing/permutation work.
- We should not assume “GMM is slow” until the profile explicitly splits:
  - router / top-k
  - token counting / prefix sums
  - permute / dispatch / gather
  - expert input matmul(s)
  - activation
  - expert output matmul(s)
  - unpermute / combine / scatter
  - residual reshards / collectives
  - cross entropy

Recommended next profile work:

1. Add or verify semantic `jax.named_scope` coverage around the MoE internals listed above. The current profile often has useful high-level scopes but not enough detail for the kernels after the obvious fwd+bwd blocks.
2. Relaunch a single-node B8 SGD readable profile with command buffers disabled for profiling only:
   - Use `--xla_gpu_enable_command_buffer=''` to preserve name-stack visibility.
   - Expect this to hurt performance; do not compare its MFU directly against production runs. Use it for attribution.
3. Build a phase table from the readable profile:
   - wall time per phase
   - kernel count per phase
   - collective count / bytes per phase
   - dot/GEMM kernel shapes if recoverable from HLO/profiler metadata
   - achieved TFLOP/s for expert matmul phases
4. Run two small ablations if attribution is still unclear:
   - Fake or bypass expert matmuls while keeping routing/permutation, to measure movement/layout overhead.
   - Fake or bypass routing/permutation while preserving representative expert matmul shapes, to measure GMM ceiling.
5. Separately evaluate Pallas fused softmax-xent against XLA CE on this exact single-node shape. XLA CE has shown suspicious tiny-fusion behavior in prior profiles and may be a meaningful non-MoE tax.
6. Keep MaxText/Hopper flag testing as a secondary lane. Flags may buy something, but they are unlikely to explain the whole 16 MFU gap without the phase attribution above.

Working hypothesis to test, not assume:

- The non-optimizer bottleneck is probably inside the MoE block plus cross entropy, but the MoE portion could be either expert compute or permute/unpermute/layout movement.
- The most important immediate deliverable is a profile where the MoE region is semantically decomposed enough that we can say which of those it is.

Suggested success criterion for this handoff:

- Produce a single-node B8 SGD profile and table that can answer: “Of the ~0.438s May141 step, how much is attention, CE, router/permute/unpermute, expert matmul/GMM, dense non-MoE compute, and collectives/reshards?”
- Only after that should we prioritize either better GMM kernels, a routing/permutation rewrite, Pallas CE, or less remat.

comments.author: dlwh
comments.body:
🤖 DeepEP internode smoke update (2026-06-21):

Short version: DeepEP does support cross-node, but our current Levanter/JAX integration does not yet have a working cross-node DeepEP runtime. The upstream normal internode path is built around one process per GPU; our smoke is one JAX process per 8-GPU node.

What changed:
- Fixed deterministic NVSHMEM package/lib discovery so both nodes use cu13/r13 instead of one node finding r12.9 and the other r13.0.
- Bumped the DeepEP FFI cache key to v37.
- Matched the smoke config to upstream normal-mode internode config: num_sms=24, NVL send/recv=8/512, RDMA send/recv=16/128.
- Increased smoke runtime buffers from 8MiB/8MiB to 512MiB NVL / 128MiB RDMA.
- Added a C++ workspace preflight before notify_dispatch.

Smoke results:
- /dlwh/deepep-internode-dispatch-smoke-20260621-070308: initialized successfully with larger buffers, reached notify_dispatch on all 16 ranks, then every rank timed out waiting for recv counters; counters stayed -1 and CUDA teardown reported illegal address.
- /dlwh/deepep-internode-dispatch-smoke-20260621-071217: adding the full upstream NVSHMEM env bundle hung at nvshmem_init_begin; stopped.
- /dlwh/deepep-internode-dispatch-smoke-20260621-071926: narrowed env to IBGDA/QP/granularity only, still hung at nvshmem_init_begin; stopped.

Current interpretation:
- The mixed NVSHMEM runtime issue is fixed.
- Buffer undersizing was not the root cause of the notify counter timeout.
- Enabling IBGDA in our one-process-per-node runtime hangs during NVSHMEM init. Without IBGDA, init succeeds but notify_dispatch likely hits the IBGDA-dependent kernel path and corrupts/fails before writing counters.
- This points to a runtime-model mismatch: upstream DeepEP’s working normal internode path uses torch.multiprocessing with one process per local GPU; our host-call smoke tries to drive all 8 local GPUs from one JAX process.

Likely next steps:
1. Prove upstream DeepEP internode works on this CoreWeave cluster using its native one-process-per-GPU test harness, if feasible in the image.
2. Decide whether we can/want to run the model in a one-process-per-GPU shape, or instead implement the DeepEP idea with JAX/NCCL/Pallas collectives that fit one-process-per-node.
3. If staying one-process-per-node, stop trying to directly call upstream normal-mode internode kernels until we have a credible multi-GPU-per-process NVSHMEM/IBGDA design.

comments.body:
🤖 EP16 padded all-to-all update.

# Issue 4312 EP16 padded all-to-all probe

Date: 2026-06-21

## Runs

| Backend | Run | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ring` | `GM2560-MAY-227S4096-W2048-B16-R1-E16M1-PALLASCE-RING-FA4SGD-SHAPEPROBE-N2-cw-20260621-0817` | Completed |
| `ragged_all_to_all` | `GM2560-MAY-228S4096-W2048-B16-R1-E16M1-PALLASCE-RAGGEDA2A-FA4SGD-SHAPEPROBE-N2-cw-20260621-0818` | Training/profile completed; W&B finish crashed |
| `padded_all_to_all` | `GM2560-MAY-229S4096-W2048-B16-R1-E16M1-PALLASCE-PADDEDA2A-FA4SGD-SHAPEPROBE-N2-cw-20260621-0841` | Invalid: stopped after step 0 with NaN loss |
| `padded_all_to_all` with sender bucket clipping | `GM2560-MAY-230S4096-W2048-B16-R1-E16M1-PALLASCE-PADDEDA2ACLIP-FA4SGD-SHAPEPROBE-N2-cw-20260621-0853` | Completed training/profile; W&B finish crashed after artifact upload |

## Local fix

The first padded attempt exposed a correctness bug in the fixed-bucket layout:
`per_peer_capacity = ceil(receiver_capacity / ep_size)` is an average capacity.
If one sender sends more than that to one destination, kept assignments can
write past their fixed bucket and corrupt later buckets. I fixed this by
clipping each sender-to-destination expert block to `per_peer_capacity` before
packing.

Local CPU multi-device reproduction:

| Capacity factor | Padded drops | Ring drops | Padded NaNs | Max finite diff |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1.0 | 2 | 1 | 0 | 0.2534 |
| 1.25 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0.0156 |
| 2.0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0.0156 |

The stricter fixed bucket can drop more than ring at capacity factor 1.0. That
means a production version either needs a launch/configurable capacity factor,
dynamic bucket sizing, or a different packing policy.

## Throughput

May230 stayed finite and produced usable rows:

| Step | Critical duration | Critical tokens/s | Critical MFU |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 2 | 0.0948s | 691k | 18.78 |
| 3 | 0.1323s | 495k | 13.45 |
| 4 | 0.1317s | 498k | 13.52 |
| 5 | 0.1100s | 596k | 16.18 |

For comparison, the previous profile-window references were:

| Backend | Step 5 critical duration | Step 5 average MFU |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `ring` | ~0.085s | ~21.34 |
| `ragged_all_to_all` | ~0.0966s | ~18.50 |
| clipped `padded_all_to_all` | ~0.110s | ~16.25 |

So the fixed-bucket path is correct enough to run but slower than both previous
EP16 baselines.

## Profile comparison

Profile summaries:

- Ring: `scratch/profile_reports/issue4312_ep16_may227_ring/summary.json`
- Ragged: `scratch/profile_reports/issue4312_ep16_may228_ragged/summary.json`
- Padded clipped: `scratch/profile_reports/issue4312_ep16_may230_padded_clip/summary.json`

Kernel-duration breakdown:

| Backend | Compute | Communication | Total kernel duration |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `ring` | 917.8 ms (60.1%) | 609.2 ms (39.9%) | 1527.0 ms |
| `ragged_all_to_all` | 899.2 ms (56.0%) | 706.4 ms (44.0%) | 1605.6 ms |
| clipped `padded_all_to_all` | 1019.1 ms (51.9%) | 943.3 ms (48.1%) | 1962.4 ms |

Collective totals:

| Backend | Collective | Count | Total time | Avg time |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `ring` | all-gather | 192 | 254.9 ms | 1.33 ms |
| `ring` | all-reduce | 272 | 211.0 ms | 0.78 ms |
| `ring` | reduce-scatter | 128 | 143.3 ms | 1.12 ms |
| `ragged_all_to_all` | send-recv | 768 | 388.0 ms | 0.51 ms |
| `ragged_all_to_all` | all-reduce | 272 | 279.6 ms | 1.03 ms |
| `ragged_all_to_all` | all-gather | 64 | 38.8 ms | 0.61 ms |
| clipped `padded_all_to_all` | send-recv | 256 | 701.3 ms | 2.74 ms |
| clipped `padded_all_to_all` | all-reduce | 272 | 229.1 ms | 0.84 ms |
| clipped `padded_all_to_all` | all-gather | 64 | 12.9 ms | 0.20 ms |

The padded path did reduce send/recv launch count relative to ragged (256 vs
768), but each send/recv got much more expensive. The largest individual rows
are the padded combine and dispatch all-to-alls:

- `moe_ep_padded_a2a/combine_transport/all_to_all`: 64 calls, 342.3 ms total,
  5.35 ms average.
- `moe_ep_padded_a2a/dispatch/all_to_all`: 64 calls, 185.1 ms total,
  2.89 ms average.
- Reverse/pass counterparts add another ~174 ms.

## Takeaway

This padded all-to-all variant is not a win as implemented. It validates the
idea that launch-count reduction alone is not enough: the fixed bucket payloads
are too fat, especially on combine. Next useful directions:

1. Add a configurable MoE capacity factor and rerun padded at 1.25 to separate
   bucket overflow/drop behavior from transport cost.
2. Try packed variable-size buckets with fewer launches but without padding to
   the average fixed bucket shape.
3. Keep pursuing DeepEP/NVSHMEM internode bring-up or a lower-level bridge, since
   the ideal target is still packed expert traffic without this much padding.

comments.body:
🤖 DeepEP internode bridge plan for issue #4312, 2026-06-21

Current measured state:

- EP16/N2 ring remains the fastest measured backend for the 4-layer shape probe.
- Assigned-token succeeded but underperformed ring:
  - May232 assigned-token step 5: 18.07/18.13 MFU across the two tasks.
  - May227 ring step 5: 21.79/20.88 MFU.
  - Assigned-token profile: send-recv 1024 / 436.3 ms, all-reduce 272 / 324.6 ms, all-gather 64 / 95.9 ms.
- Therefore assigned-token is not the right cross-node replacement for ring on this shape.

DeepEP state in this branch:

- `lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/ep_deepep.py` imports and calls only:
  - `deepep_dispatch_intranode`
  - `deepep_dispatch_intranode_with_assignments`
  - `deepep_combine_intranode`
- `lib/levanter/src/levanter/kernels/deepep/transport_ffi.py` has internode runtime/bootstrap helpers:
  - `ensure_internode_runtime`
  - `internode_runtime_status`
  - `run_host_internode_dispatch_round`
- `lib/levanter/src/levanter/kernels/deepep/csrc/deepep_transport_ffi.cu` has a host-only `levanter_deepep_run_host_internode_dispatch_round` that calls upstream `deep_ep::internode::notify_dispatch` and `deep_ep::internode::dispatch`.
- There is no jitted XLA FFI target for internode dispatch/combine returning JAX arrays, and the Grug MoE backend does not have an internode DeepEP branch.

Interpretation:

- Upstream DeepEP supports cross-node. Marin's current JAX training-facing backend does not.
- The missing piece is not a launch flag. It is a real XLA FFI wrapper for the internode path plus Python wrappers and a Grug backend selection path.

Pragmatic implementation ladder:

1. Prove host internode smoke on CoreWeave with NVSHMEM/IBGDA enabled.
   - Use `ensure_internode_runtime(...)`.
   - Call `run_host_internode_dispatch_round(...)` on a 2-node job.
   - If this fails, fix runtime/NVSHMEM/CoreWeave env first.

2. Add an explicit internode dispatch FFI target in `deepep_transport_ffi.cu`.
   - Inputs should mirror intranode dispatch plus RDMA-rank counts:
     - `x`, `topk_idx`, `topk_weights`
     - `num_tokens_per_rank`
     - `num_tokens_per_rdma_rank`
     - `num_tokens_per_expert`
     - `is_token_in_rank`
   - Outputs need to include at least:
     - `recv_x`
     - `recv_topk_idx`
     - `recv_topk_weights`
     - source metadata for combine, not just `recv_src_idx`
     - RDMA/global prefix matrices and prefix sums
     - `send_rdma_head`, `send_nvl_head`
     - local expert counts / recv counts
   - Use the host smoke implementation as the source of the exact upstream API call sequence.

3. Add Python wrappers in `transport_ffi.py`.
   - `deepep_dispatch_internode(...)`
   - later `deepep_combine_internode(...)`
   - Keep intranode wrappers unchanged.

4. Add a Grug backend variant only after the dispatch/combine wrappers exist.
   - Avoid pretending `deepep` is cross-node until both dispatch and combine work under `jit(train_step)`.
   - The backend must be effectful/remat-aware like current `deepep` and `deepep_composed`.

comments.body:
🤖 DeepEP/CoreWeave internode smoke update, 2026-06-21

Short answer: yes, upstream DeepEP is cross-node capable. The gap is Marin integration, not DeepEP itself.

I ran the upstream DeepEP 2-node internode test on CoreWeave and got it passing after two env fixes:

- Use Iris/NCCL's exact routable ethernet interface for NVSHMEM UID bootstrap: `NVSHMEM_BOOTSTRAP_UID_SOCK_IFNAME="=enp157s0np0"`. Without this, NVSHMEM UID bootstrap picked bad/default `ib*` paths and timed out.
- Point NVSHMEM IBGDA at CoreWeave's HCA prefix: `NVSHMEM_HCA_PREFIX=ibp`. Without this, NVSHMEM skipped `ibp0..ibp7` because it expected default `mlx5`, then DeepEP dispatch timed out.

Successful job:

- `/dlwh/deepep-upstream-internode-test-hcaprefix-20260621-101712`
- 2 H100 nodes on `cw-us-east-02a`
- Both tasks succeeded in ~92s.
- Env snapshot confirmed `NVSHMEM_BOOTSTRAP_UID_SOCK_IFNAME="=enp157s0np0"`, `NVSHMEM_HCA_PREFIX="ibp"`, `NVSHMEM_IB_ENABLE_IBGDA=1`.
- Upstream test reached layout and passed BF16/FP8 dispatch/combine variants, including async/previous-token cases.

This means the CoreWeave/NVSHMEM/IBGDA runtime path is viable. Remaining work is to wire a real JAX/XLA FFI internode dispatch/combine path into Marin/Grug; current `deepep` / `deepep_composed` training backends still call intranode wrappers only.

comments.author: dlwh
comments.body:
🤖 DeepEP internode JAX follow-up, 2026-06-21

Short answer to the confusion: yes, upstream DeepEP is cross-node. The current blocker is that Marin/JAX is not running DeepEP in the same process/device model that upstream assumes.

What I verified today:

- Upstream DeepEP normal-mode internode already passed on CoreWeave with the right NVSHMEM env.
- Marin's JAX internode FFI now builds and static contract tests pass.
- The JAX smoke with the restored single RDMA allocation reaches internode runtime init, but dispatch stalls in the receive-counter handshake.
- I then tried the obvious fix: allocate one NVSHMEM/RDMA buffer per local GPU runtime inside Marin's one-process-per-node JAX process. That failed earlier: NVSHMEM init succeeded, the first per-local-rank allocation returned, then `cudaMemset(internode rdma buffer)` failed with `invalid argument`.

Interpretation:

- Upstream normal-mode DeepEP uses 16 GPU ranks for 2 nodes, but collapses NVSHMEM ranks to 2 RDMA/node ranks.
- Even with collapsed NVSHMEM ranks, upstream still has one process per GPU rank, each with its own CUDA device context and `Buffer` sync path.
- Marin's JAX job has one process per node controlling 8 GPUs. That appears incompatible with DeepEP's NVSHMEM ownership assumptions for the normal-mode internode path.
- This is an integration/process-model problem, not evidence that DeepEP cannot do cross-node or that CoreWeave networking is broken.

I updated `scratch/profile_reports/issue4312_deepep_status_20260621.md` with the run id and details. The worktree is restored to the prior single-RDMA-allocation path after the experiment, so static validation is back to passing:

```bash
uv run python -m py_compile lib/levanter/src/levanter/kernels/deepep/transport_ffi.py
uv run pytest lib/levanter/tests/kernels/test_deepep_availability.py -q
```

Result: `28 passed, 11 warnings`.

Likely next directions are either: make the DeepEP path run in a one-process-per-GPU execution model, keep DeepEP intranode-only and build a JAX-native cross-node EP transport, or port more of DeepEP's normal-mode algorithm into a JAX-compatible custom transport that does not rely on NVSHMEM owning one CUDA device per process.

comments.body:
🤖 Update: May-shape batch/remat, O1, and PGLE-no-O1 probes

Scope for this batch: May d2560/L26 shape, ring MoE, SGD fwd/bwd, FA4, Pallas CE, bf16 params/compute/output, `model_axis=1`, `expert_axis=8`, synthetic data, no checkpoints.

Main result:
- B8/device is not runnable in this config. No-flags `save_moe` OOMed at ~120-122 GiB/device; no-flags `recompute_all` still OOMed at 93.15 GiB on N2.

- The JAX Toolbox/O1 flag bundle is a slowdown at the runnable size, not a win.
- AutoPGLE without O1 gives only a tiny final-step improvement and worse mean MFU. Both PGLE runs warned `PGLE collected an empty trace`, so I would not treat these as a healthy PGLE success yet.

| Run | Nodes | Flags | Batch/device | Remat | Final MFU | Mean MFU | Tokens/s | Duration |
| --- | ---: | --- | ---: | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| [May402](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/GM2560-MAY-402S4096-W2048-B64-R2-E8M1-PALLASCE-RING-RECOMPUTEALL-FA4SGD-NOFLAGS-N2-cw-20260624-020812) | 2 | none | 4 | `recompute_all` | 20.6288 | 15.5391 | 190,767 | 1.374s |

| [May404](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/GM2560-MAY-404S4096-W2048-B64-R2-E8M1-PALLASCE-RING-RECOMPUTEALL-FA4SGD-JAXTOOLBOXO1-N2-cw-20260624-023445) | 2 | O1/toolbox | 4 | `recompute_all` | 18.3573 | 13.7808 | 169,761 | 1.544s |
| [May405](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/GM2560-MAY-405S4096-W2048-B64-R2-E8M1-PALLASCE-RING-RECOMPUTEALL-FA4SGD-PGLE-N2-cw-20260624-032705) | 2 | PGLE, no O1 | 4 | `recompute_all` | 21.3041 | 15.0287 | 197,012 | 1.331s |
| [May406](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/GM2560-MAY-406S4096-W2048-B128-R4-E8M1-PALLASCE-RING-RECOMPUTEALL-FA4SGD-PGLE-N4-cw-20260624-032718) | 4 | PGLE, no O1 | 4 | `recompute_all` | 20.1182 | 14.3038 | 372,090 | 1.409s |

OOM boundary notes:
- May396/May397: B8/device, `save_moe`, no flags, OOMed on first train step at ~120.37 GiB N2 and ~122.23 GiB N4.
- May398: B8/device, `recompute_all`, no flags, OOMed on first train step allocating 93.15 GiB.
- May399: B4/device, `save_moe`, no flags, OOMed on first train step allocating 56.39 GiB.
- Earlier May392/May393 O1/toolbox B8/device `save_moe` also OOMed at ~124 GiB, but the no-flags controls show that larger shape is already over memory.

Interpretation:
- Use no-flags B4/device + `recompute_all` as the stable baseline for this lane.
- Do not carry the O1/JAX Toolbox flag bundle for now; at the runnable N2 size it regressed final MFU/tokens by ~11% and increased duration by ~12% versus May402.

- N4 roughly doubles tokens/sec versus N2 but MFU is flat/slightly lower, and 32-device startup was flaky with repeated clique/rendezvous retries before May403 completed.

spillover_issues.author: ClassicLarry
spillover_issues.body:
🤖 **Depth scaling at fixed width (d512)** — does adding layers + data track the width scaling law, where does the per-layer gradient go with depth, and can we lift the starved early-layer experts.

### Initiating prompts (user)
> lets take the d512 baseline moe, and run it again with 12, 18, and 24 layers. Scale data volume by 2x, 3x, 4x.

> lets take our 4 fasttrack-moe baselines, and plot out the grad at the midpoint in training as a function of layer depth ... I want to see if early layers have a smaller grad

> follow agent.md and make an issue for depth scaling ... [+ depth-study per-layer grads, attn-gate norm per run, attn-residuals + loss comparison]

> lets try the idea from [alltoall notion, "save lower-layer moe experts"] ... apply an auxiliary loss to the output of the first layer for the first 1k steps ... aux loss 0.1 at init, decay linear to 0 over 1k steps ... another version 3k steps. Run both for all 4 sizes of the d512 [depth] ladder.

### Setup
- fast_track MoE, `hero-bpe-v16384` (vocab 16384), SEQ_LEN 4096, 8×H100 (1 node), data-matched, project `marin-community/marin_moe`.
- **Depth ladder** — d512 at 6/12/18/24 layers, token budget 1×/2×/3×/4× (`--num-layers` × `--data-mult`). **Width ladder** — `fasttrack-moe-{d512..d1280}`.
- Metric: `eval/paloma/macro_loss` (final).

## 1. Depth scaling vs the width scaling law
![depth vs width scaling](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/07c38ee51efa40fb38ad833d613ccd24390d6fb4/experiments/grug/fast_track/depth_scaling/depth_vs_width_scaling.png)

Width fit `L = 1.2 + 58.97·C^(−0.0843)` (matches README `1.2 + 58.67·C^(−0.0842)`). The d512 depth ladder lands on the width compute-efficiency frontier, with a small penalty growing to +0.014 macro loss by L24.

| ladder | config | layers | FLOPs | Paloma | vs law |
|---|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| depth | d512 1× | 6 | 3.46e17 | 3.156 | −0.002 |
| depth | d512 2× | 12 | 1.23e18 | 2.963 | +0.004 |
| depth | d512 3× | 18 | 2.69e18 | 2.860 | +0.013 |
| depth | d512 4× | 24 | 4.65e18 | 2.787 | +0.014 |
| width | d768 | 8 | 2.28e18 | 2.872 | — |
| width | d1024 | 12 | 1.41e19 | 2.633 | — |
| width | d1280 | 14 | 4.26e19 | 2.504 | — |

## 2. Per-layer gradient magnitude over depth
Width baselines: ![grad by depth — width](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/07c38ee51efa40fb38ad833d613ccd24390d6fb4/experiments/grug/fast_track/depth_scaling/grad_norm_by_depth.png)
Depth study: ![grad by depth — depth](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/07c38ee51efa40fb38ad833d613ccd24390d6fb4/experiments/grug/fast_track/depth_scaling/depth_grad_norm_by_layer.png)

Routed experts monotone-increasing with depth (smallest at layer 0); shared flat + final spike; attention mid-hump then collapses at the deepest layer. Consistent across width and depth. (Caveat: routed experts train under Muon + load-balancing, so small grad-norm ≠ undertrained by itself.)

Attention-gate param norm by layer: ![attn gate norm](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/07c38ee51efa40fb38ad833d613ccd24390d6fb4/experiments/grug/fast_track/depth_scaling/attn_gate_param_norm.png) — deeper models push the early-layer attention gate harder.

## 3. Kimi Attention Residuals (exploratory)
Reverses the deep-layer attention-grad collapse (attn grad stays high/peaks at depth): ![AttnRes attn grad](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/07c38ee51efa40fb38ad833d613ccd24390d6fb4/experiments/grug/fast_track/depth_scaling/attn_residuals_attention_grad.png)
Full redistribution (std solid vs AttnRes dashed, matched midpoint step): ![AttnRes grad](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/07c38ee51efa40fb38ad833d613ccd24390d6fb4/experiments/grug/fast_track/depth_scaling/attn_residuals_grad_by_depth.png)
Loss (all final): AttnRes beats standard at every depth — L12 2.953 vs 2.963, L18 2.855 vs 2.860, **L24 2.775 vs 2.787** (−0.005 to −0.012); small but consistent (parked). ![AttnRes loss](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/07c38ee51efa40fb38ad833d613ccd24390d6fb4/experiments/grug/fast_track/depth_scaling/attn_residuals_loss_comparison.png)

## 4. First-layer auxiliary loss ("save lower-layer experts")
Read block 0's output through the shared LM head, add a next-token CE weighted **0.1 → 0 linearly over 1k or 3k steps**. Run on the d512 depth ladder (6/12/18/24). Question: does early supervision leave the first layer with durably higher gradient, and does it help loss?

**Layer-0 gradient over training** (L6 washes out — too short; L12 persists after decay): ![aux layer0 grad](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/07c38ee51efa40fb38ad833d613ccd24390d6fb4/experiments/grug/fast_track/depth_scaling/aux_layer0_grad.png)

**Routed experts specifically — the effect is large and lasting** (layer-0 routed grad, normally the smallest in the net, stays multiples above plain after decay): ![aux layer0 routed](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/07c38ee51efa40fb38ad833d613ccd24390d6fb4/experiments/grug/fast_track/depth_scaling/aux_layer0_routed_grad.png)

| post-decay (5k→end) | plain | aux1k | aux3k |
|---|---|---|---|
| L18 | 0.0027 | 0.0077 (2.9×) | 0.0135 (5.0×) |
| L24 | 0.0015 | 0.0051 (3.4×) | 0.0103 (6.9×) |

**Routed grad, full profile by layer** — the boost is localized to the first ~2–4 layers, flattening the starved early end; deep layers unchanged: ![aux routed profile](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/07c38ee51efa40fb38ad833d613ccd24390d6fb4/experiments/grug/fast_track/depth_scaling/aux_routed_grad_profile.png)

**Attention-gate norm by layer** — the supervised first layer shifts work away from its attention gate (layer-0 gate norm drops, L24: 3.75→2.08 aux3k), only at layer 0: ![aux attn gate](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/07c38ee51efa40fb38ad833d613ccd24390d6fb4/experiments/grug/fast_track/depth_scaling/aux_attn_gate_profile.png)

**Final train loss — the aux is a small win at depth.** Final cross-entropy (last-30-step avg): the aux is slightly *better* than plain at L12/L18/L24 and a hair worse at L6.

| depth | plain | aux1k | aux3k |
|---|---|---|---|
| L6  | 2.065 | 2.069 | 2.069 |
| L12 | 1.910 | 1.904 | 1.902 |
| L18 | 1.800 | 1.790 | 1.789 |
| L24 | 1.748 | 1.743 | 1.742 |

So the gradient rebalancing comes with a small (−0.006 to −0.011) final-train-loss improvement at depth — modest, and aux3k ≈ aux1k. The raw eval/paloma numbers were inflated by an eval-time bug (loss called with `step=None` → aux applied at full weight at eval, +~0.1×first-layer-CE); fixed so eval reports pure CE (training was always correct).

**Net:** the aux durably rebalances the early blocks from attention-gating toward routed-expert compute — a real gradient/utilization effect that scales with depth and duration — but it did **not** move final loss at these settings.

## 5. AttnRes tuning — from marginal to a real win

The first AttnRes pass gave only ~0.01 macro loss. Investigating the optimizer routing revealed the per-layer pseudo-queries were being **MuonH-updated** (scan-stacking makes each `[num_layers, d]` query a 2D leaf, which the shape-based `create_mask` sent to MuonH). Fixing that — route queries to **Adam**, **zero-init** them (uniform depth-attention at init), a **parameter-free key norm** (the learnable gain is redundant with the query), and a **lower query LR** — turned AttnRes into a solid ~0.05 win. All d512, N=8, data-matched; Paloma macro loss (final), lower better.

**Tuning progression at L12 (each row adds one change):**

| # | config | Paloma | Δ vs baseline |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| 0 | baseline (no AttnRes) | 2.963 | — |
| 1 | + AttnRes, query on **MuonH**, rand-init, learnable key-norm | 2.953 | −0.010 |
| 2 | query → **Adam** group (rand-init) | 2.951 | −0.012 |
| 3 | + **zero-init** query | 2.935 | −0.028 |
| 4 | + **param-free** key-norm (neutral, as predicted) | 2.935 | −0.028 |
| 5 | + query **LR 0.1×** | 2.916 | −0.047 |
| 6 | + query **LR 0.05×** (best) | 2.915 | **−0.048** |

Zero-init is the single biggest lever; the param-free key-norm is neutral (confirming the gain is absorbed by the query); the query LR wants to be ~0.05–0.1× the adam LR.

**Query-LR sweep** (config = zero-init query + param-free key-norm):

![AttnRes query-LR sweep](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/07c38ee51efa40fb38ad833d613ccd24390d6fb4/experiments/grug/fast_track/depth_scaling/attnres_qlr_sweep.png)

| query LR × | L6 Paloma | L12 Paloma |
|---|---:|---:|
| baseline (no AttnRes) | 3.156 | 2.963 |
| 1.0 | 3.146 | 2.935 |
| 0.5 | 3.137 | 2.931 |
| 0.3 | 3.136 | 2.921 |
| **0.1** | **3.130** | 2.916 |
| **0.05** | 3.134 | **2.915** |
| 0.01 | 3.135 | 2.924 |

**Config ablation across depths** (final Paloma; "run" = still training):

| depth | baseline | MuonH-q | Adam-q rand | Adam-q **zero** | best (zero + pfkn + qlr) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| L6  | 3.156 | — | 3.156 | 3.145 | **3.130** (0.1×) |
| L12 | 2.963 | 2.953 | 2.951 | 2.935 | **2.915** (0.05×) |
| L18 | 2.860 | 2.855 | 2.854 | **2.820** | (qlr not run) |
| L24 | 2.787 | 2.775 | run | run | — |

Zero-init query alone is a large jump at depth (L18 −0.040 vs baseline; L12 −0.028). The query-LR sweep (L6/L12 only so far) adds another ~0.02. Deeper zero-init runs (L24) and L48 across configs are still training; qlr sweep at L18/L24 is the natural next step.

Plots + data under `experiments/grug/fast_track/depth_scaling/` (branch `depth-scaling-analysis`, commit `ec38f6fe30`). Feature commits on `fast-track-first-layer-aux`.

comments.author: ClassicLarry

🤖 **Tuned AttnRes lifts the early-layer routed-expert gradient (d512, 12 layers)**

Per-layer routed-expert grad norm at the training midpoint (100-step avg, steps ~2335–2435 of 4770), for the best tuned config `ft-attnres-pfkn-qlr005-d512-L12` (zero-init query, parameter-free key-norm, query LR 0.05× → Paloma **2.915** vs baseline **2.963**) against the plain-residual baseline `ft-d512-L12-data2x`.

![tuned AttnRes routed grad by layer](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/a5dac3837b63e37701aea942e22b353c1e38065d/experiments/grug/fast_track/depth_scaling/attnres_tuned_routed_grad_L12.png)

| layer | baseline | AttnRes tuned |
|---|---:|---:|
| 0 | 0.0049 | **0.0134** (2.7×) |
| 1 | 0.0140 | **0.0214** (1.5×) |
| 2 | 0.0194 | 0.0177 |
| 3–8 | ~0.020–0.023 | ~0.017–0.024 (≈ equal) |
| 11 (last) | 0.0318 | 0.0282 |

The baseline routed-grad ramps steeply from a tiny layer-0 up to the late layers; tuned AttnRes **lifts layers 0–1** (layer 0 ~2.7×), merges with baseline by layer ~3, and is slightly lower at the deepest layer. So AttnRes gives the first-layer routed experts much more gradient — the same "save the lower-layer experts" behaviour as the first-layer aux loss — **but here it also improves loss** (−0.048 macro, ≈1.39× compute-efficient per the fast_track law), whereas the aux loss lifted the gradient without a loss win.

Routed = quadrature of `grad/norm/stacked_blocks.<i>.{mlp.*, mlp_gated_norm, rms_mlp, sconv_mlp}`. Data committed at `a5dac3837b` under `experiments/grug/fast_track/depth_scaling/`.

spillover_issues.author: ClassicLarry
spillover_issues.body:
🤖 **Experiment:** Ephemeral MoE — a decaying "scratchpad" residual channel.

**Prompt that initiated this:**
> try an idea called Ephemeral MoE. Each Expert should project out to a latent of size hidden, instead of size hidden/2. Then after returning to the home GPU, the full length latent should be broken into 2 halves. The first half projects to the full hidden_dim and acts as the normal output. The second half projects out to the hidden dim and acts as the ephemeral output. First, we add the normal output to the residual stream x. Then we calc ephemeral_loss = eph_stream*lambda. Then x -= eph_loss; eph_stream -= eph_loss; eph_stream += eph_output. x+=eph_output. The idea is that whatever gets added to the ephemeral output will decay out of the residual stream with some specified halflife determined by lambda. So neurons can choose 'I am writing something that should stick around and predict the final output' vs 'I am writing something temporary to the scratchpad'. eph_stream is init to zero. Run at d512 and d768. Do a version where lambda is learnable, init to 1. And a version where lambda is hardcoded to 0.5.

**Mechanism (verified):** `eph_stream_t = (1-λ)·eph_stream_{t-1} + eph_out_t`; `x`'s ephemeral component stays exactly equal to `eph_stream`, and an ephemeral write fully cancels out of `x` over depth (`λ·Σ(1-λ)^k = 1`), leaving `(1-λ)^{T-i}` at the output — late writes persist, early writes decay. Halflife `= ln0.5/ln(1-λ)` layers.

**Design:** MoE, d512 + d768, **data-matched** to the MoE baseline (macro loss d512 3.156 / d768 2.872). **λ = sigmoid(raw)** for stability (per the review). Two arms:
- **learnable** λ (init ≈1, per layer, logged to `eph_moe/lambda_layer_*`)
- **fixed** λ = 0.5

Caveat: not iso-param — the size-hidden expert latent + second up-proj ~2× the expert latent/up-proj params vs baseline, so this is quality-at-more-params. Branch `fast-track-attn-reinject`.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **Results + diagnosis: a small gain that looks like params, not the ephemeral mechanism.**

Both arms, d512 + d768, data-matched to the MoE baseline (`eval/paloma/macro_loss`):

| scale | baseline | eph learnable λ | Δ | eph fixed λ=0.5 | Δ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| d512 | 3.1559 | 3.1195 | −0.036 | 3.1196 | −0.036 |
| d768 | 2.8723 | 2.8384 | −0.034 | 2.8385 | −0.034 |

**Effective speedup vs baseline** (data-matched, MoE ladder fit L∞=1.2 pinned → α=0.153): **~0.85 at d512** (1.33× slower, 1.13× data-gain) and **~0.84 at d768** — i.e. slightly compute-**negative**. Not iso-param: the size-hidden expert latent + second up-proj is ~2× the expert latent/up-proj params, and the effective-speedup already charges that via throughput.

**Learned per-layer λ** (learnable arm, all init 0.98):
- d512 (6L): `[0.98, 0.748, 0.739, 0.86, 0.996, 0.996]`
- d768 (8L): `[0.98, 0.698, 0.832, 0.69, 0.861, 0.996, 0.996, 0.996]`

Halflife is **< 1 layer at every layer**, most aggressive (λ→~1) at the **final** layers — the model erases the ephemeral channel almost immediately, hardest right before the output.

**Why this reads as "not really the mechanism":**
1. **λ trained toward ~1 everywhere.** If the decaying channel carried useful multi-layer state, some layers would drop λ toward 0. None did — the model does not want a long-lived scratchpad; it deletes ephemeral writes within a layer (and slams the last layers to ~1 so scratchpad can't leak into the logits).
2. **learnable ≈ fixed-0.5** (Δ ≈ 0.0001). If the halflife mattered, tuning it would help; it doesn't. So the ephemeral *dynamics* are ~inert, and the −0.036 is coming from the extra capacity, mostly routed through the normal (permanent) channel.

So the gain ≈ "what ~2× expert params buy," with the ephemeral decay adding little on top.

**Proposed follow-ups (decisive first):**
- **Iso-param eph** — keep latent = hidden/2, split into 2×(hidden/4), each up-proj to hidden. Same params as baseline ⇒ any gain is *purely* the mechanism. (If ≈ baseline, the idea is dead; if it gains, it's real.)
- **2×-permanent control** — same 2× params, both halves added permanently (no decay). If eph ≈ this, the decay contributes nothing beyond params.
- If the mechanism survives those: **per-channel λ** (a halflife per feature dim, not one scalar/layer), **content-gated λ** (compute λ from the token), and a **24-layer test** (6–8 layers gives a scratchpad almost no distance to be useful).

Leaving the issue open pending the iso-param + 2×-permanent control at d512.

spillover_issues.title: [fast-track] Ephemeral MoE: decaying scratchpad residual channel

spillover_issues.author: ClassicLarry
spillover_issues.body:
## Summary

Test **omni-neurons**: a dense-model variant where each layer's **MLP** reads the
concatenation of *every prior sublayer snapshot* instead of just the current
residual stream. Attention is unchanged (it still reads the residual stream).

For layer `n` the MLP input is the concatenation of:
`[embed, {attn_out_i, resid_post_attn_i, mlp_out_i, resid_post_mlp_i for each prior layer i}, attn_out_n, resid_post_attn_n]`
— each `d`-wide, so the MLP input width grows with depth as `d·(4n+3)`. The MLP
still writes a `d`-wide residual delta (asymmetric in/out).

**Research goal:** after training, inspect *where the MLP input neurons point* —
do they attend to the individual layer branch outputs (`attn_out` / `mlp_out`) or
to the accumulated residual-stream sums (`resid_post_attn` / `resid_post_mlp`)?
This is why final checkpoints are saved.

## Exact prompts

> follow agent.md and test an idea called omni-neurons. Lets use the dense model as the baseline. but save the output of every layer, and the sum after its added to the residual stream. The input to layer n will then be a concatenated list of [embed, layer0_attn_out, layer0_resid_post_attn, layer0_mlp_out, layer0_resid_post_mlp, layer1_attn_out, layer1_resid_post_attn...]. So the input dim to layer I scales with the layer. EG layer 6 will have roughly 24x wider dims. First, will this fit at d512?

> oh, lets only use omni input for mlp, not attn.

> yes, run both sizes and raise a github issue. The idea here is we want to investigate after it trains where the input neurons are pointing. To see if they are looking at the layer outputs, or the residual stream sums. So we also need to turn on final checkpoint saving.

## Feasibility (MLP-only omni, d512 dense: d=512, L=6, I=1536, seq=4096, batch=128, 8×H100)

| Item | dense baseline | omni-MLP |
|---|---|---|
| Non-embed params | 18.1M | 131.3M (7.3×) |
| Total params | 34.9M | 148.1M |
| Weights + optimizer state (14 B/param, FSDP /8) | 0.06 GB/gpu | 0.26 GB/gpu |
| Retained snapshot activations (4/layer, bf16, /8) | — | 1.68 GB/gpu |
| **Total-model FLOPs/step** (incl. attn core + embed) | 1× | **~2.9×** |

Fits trivially (single-digit GB/gpu). The binding cost is compute: ~2.9× total
FLOPs → expect ~3× slower wall-clock, so the run must show a real loss gain to
net positive on effective speedup. Params grow ≈ `L²` with depth, so the full
ladder (d1024/d1280) would get much more expensive — a gate-2 consideration.

## Implementation

Branch `fast_track_omni_mlp` @ `95a2cf0a0e` (off the baseline-budget branch).

- `model.py`: `GrugModelConfig.omni_mlp` (dense-only, default off → shared path
  byte-identical). `DenseMLP.init` gains `out_dim` (wide input, `d`-wide output).
  Heterogeneous per-layer MLP widths can't be scanned, so omni blocks are held
  **unrolled** (`Transformer.omni_blocks`) with a Python-loop forward that
  accumulates the snapshot list, per-snapshot RMSNorm (shared width-`d` gain, keeps
  snapshots magnitude-comparable), concatenates, then the wide GatedNorm + MLP.
  Each layer remat'd (`eqx.filter_checkpoint`).
- `optimizer.py`: no change needed — omni's leaves route correctly
  (`w_gate/w_up/w_down` → muonh, `rms_mlp.weight` → adam, `mlp_gated_norm` → muonh).
- `launch.py`: `--omni-mlp` flag (implies `--dense`).

Verified on CPU: per-layer widths = `d·(4i+3)` in / `d` out, non-omni path intact,
optimizer routing correct, concat bookkeeping matches. GPU forward validated by the
launched runs stepping.

## Runs (gate 1: data-matched vs the dense baseline, cw-rno2a, version 2026.09.22)

| run_id | size | steps (data-match) | checkpoints |
|---|---|---|---|
| `omni-mlp-d512` | d512 | ~690 | saved (final) |
| `omni-mlp-d768` | d768 | (dense-d768 budget) | saved (final) |

Compare `eval/paloma/macro_loss` and `throughput/tokens_per_second` against the
`fasttrack-baseline` dense d512/d768 runs; gate 1 passes if omni beats the dense
baseline macro loss at **both** scales. Final checkpoints will be analyzed for the
per-snapshot input-weight norms (layer outputs vs residual-stream sums).

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body: 🤖 First launch hit a bug: `_apply_qb_betas` (train.py) dereferenced `model.stacked_blocks.stacked.mlp`, which is `None` for omni (blocks are held unrolled in `omni_blocks`). Since omni is dense (no router), fixed to no-op like the dense branch (commit `d700080794`). Relaunched as `omni-mlp-d512-v2` / `omni-mlp-d768-v2` (cw-rno2a, version 2026.09.22, `--save-checkpoints`).

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **Omni-neuron component ablation** — which snapshots drive the gain, and does it pay off?

Added three component-selection modes to the omni MLP (branch `fast_track_omni_mlp`, commits `fac6c595f3` / `b440292d5b` / `907f97b60e`) and ran the ladder at d512/d768, data-matched, vs the dense baseline. Metric: `eval/paloma/macro_loss`.

| variant (omni MLP input) | d512 | Δ | d768 | Δ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| **dense baseline** | 3.6758 | — | 3.2825 | — |
| embed_only (`embed + x_post_attn`, width `2d`) | 3.6325 | −0.043 | 3.2481 | −0.034 |
| outputs-only (`attn_out + mlp_out`; no embed/residual) | 3.6355 | −0.040 | **7.2336** | **diverged** |
| residual-only (`embed + resid_post_attn + resid_post_mlp`) | 3.5819 | −0.094 | 3.1904 | −0.092 |
| outputs + embed (`embed + attn_out + mlp_out`) | 3.5739 | −0.102 | 3.1868 | −0.096 |
| omni-ALL (all four snapshots + embed) | 3.5534 | −0.122 | 3.1735 | −0.109 |

**Findings (consistent across both scales):**
- **omni-ALL is best** (−0.122 / −0.109) but the gain leans on a *combination* of the token identity (`embed`) and the inter-layer history — neither alone does much: `embed_only` −0.03/−0.04, and outputs-without-embed even less.
- **outputs+embed ≈ residual-only** (both ≈ −0.09 to −0.10). Once the MLP has embed + history, sublayer *outputs* and residual-*states* help about equally.
- **outputs-only is not a fair ablation:** it feeds the MLP the attention *delta* (`attn_out`), not the current residual stream (`x_post_attn`) the standard MLP reads. Missing that anchor (and `embed`), it's weakest at d512 and **diverges at d768**. The essential MLP input is the current residual; a fair "output-history" variant would keep `x_post_attn` as the base and add output deltas on top.

**But it is not compute-efficient.** Effective speedup vs dense at d768 (data-matched wall-clock to reach the variant's loss; dense loss-vs-tokens fit `L∞=1.63, α=0.193`):

| variant d768 | loss | tok/s | slower | data-gain | **eff. speedup** |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| dense | 3.2825 | 2,734,245 | — | — | — |
| omni-ALL | 3.1735 | 506,760 | 5.4× | 1.42× | **0.26** |
| outputs+embed | 3.1868 | 365,071 | 7.5× | 1.36× | **0.18** |

The quality gain is worth only ~1.4× data, nowhere near enough to offset the 5–7× throughput hit from the wide, depth-growing (`d·(4n+3)`) concat MLP → **net ~4–5× slower wall-clock**, and worsening with scale.

**Caveats:** single runs, no seeds (~±0.01–0.02 noise) — the tiers are robust, the small gaps aren't. Throughput here is node/contention-sensitive (outputs+embed measured *slower* than the wider omni-ALL, which is backwards — measurement noise); a back-to-back MFU probe would give clean throughput.

**Verdict:** a real, reproducible quality gain that localizes to *embed + inter-layer history acting together* (with the residual stream as the key MLP input), but not a compute win. The interesting follow-up is the clean matched-factorial (`base = embed + x_post_attn`, add output- vs residual-history on top) to decompose the history contribution without the outputs-only anchoring artifact.

comments.body:
42% data efficiency gain just from having access to earlier representations is interesting.. There is the direction of attention residuals where you compress these all down into hidden_dim values via some dynamic weighting. The gain after doing that is much smaller. 

Very high dimensional input space makes it easier for the neurons to target the exact input data they want. However we of course pay for this with flops. MoE is about sparsely activating neurons. Is there an inverse where we sparsely query a vast input space? Need better logging of what manifold the activations sit on to get a better sense if querying subset makes any sense.

spillover_issues.body:
🤖 **Experiment:** learnable per-layer re-injection of the attention output after the MLP.

**Prompt that initiated this:**
> lets try a new issue where we save the attn output, then after each mlp, we let the residual stream x be x + lambda*attn_output. So the model can learn to upscale, or delete out the info it pulled in from the most recent attn. Make sure the scalars (1 per layer), are plotted on wandb. run it at d512 and d768 on the moe baseline.

**Change** (`experiments/grug/fast_track/model.py`, `Block`): after the MLP residual add, re-inject the block's own attention output scaled by a learnable per-layer scalar:
```
x = x + attn_out           # post-attn residual (unchanged)
...
x = x + mlp_out            # post-mlp residual (unchanged)
x = x + attn_reinject_lambda * attn_out   # NEW: learnable re-injection
```
`attn_reinject_lambda` is one scalar per layer, init **0** (so the model starts identical to the MoE baseline) and routed to the `adam` group. It lets the model amplify (`λ>0`) or subtract out (`λ<0`) the information the most recent attention pulled in, *after* the MLP has read it. Per-layer values are logged to W&B under `attn_reinject/lambda_layer_*`. Flag: `--attn-reinject`. Default off ⇒ field is `None`, no-op, checkpoint-compatible.

**Design:** MoE, d512 and d768, data-matched to the MoE baseline. Metric: `eval/paloma/macro_loss` (baselines d512 3.156 / d768 2.872). Branch `fast-track-attn-reinject`.

spillover_issues.author: ClassicLarry
spillover_issues.body:
## TL;DR

Add and evaluate "standard" LLM architecture features on top of the fast_track MoE baseline, one
feature per branch (`fast_track_abl_<feature>`), each run at d512 and d768 and compared to the MoE
baseline (data-matched). Per agent.md, each feature gets an issue comment with its spec, branch link,
and results (Paloma/uncheatable bpb, throughput, params, FLOPs).

## Method

- Each feature is an **addition** to the current MoE baseline (not a hold-out ablation).
- Branch `fast_track_abl_<feature>` off the fast_track branch; toggle via a launcher flag/config.
- Run d512 + d768, data-matched to the MoE baseline budget (d512 = 2,385 steps, d768 = 6,930 steps,
  batch 128, seq 4096), on cw-us-east-02a. No checkpoints; eval on.
- Comment per feature: spec, branch, W&B runs, bpb (Paloma + uncheatable), throughput/MFU, params,
  FLOPs (±lm_head), 1–3 line takeaway.

## Features

### Well-specified (implementable now)
1. **MLA** — multi-head latent attention. KV latent size 512 with a learnable RMS norm; compress Q to
   512 with its own learnable RMS norm. (At d512 hidden this is ~no real compression — a structural test.)
2. **Cross-layer KV sharing** — the residual stream at the midpoint feeds KV for the final half of
   layers (every layer still keeps its own KV projection).
3. **Sandwich norm** — norm before *and* after each sublayer.
4. **Logit soft-capping** — tanh cap on attention and/or final logits.
5. **Learnable residual gain** — per-channel learnable scaling on residual adds (LayerScale-style).
6. **Parallel attention + FFN** — attention and MLP read the same block input (PaLM/GPT-J style).
7. **Tied embeddings** — share `token_embed` with `lm_head`.
8. **MTP** — multi-token prediction auxiliary head(s).

### Heavier / known but large
9. **Mamba-2** — replace ONLY the local sliding-window layers with Mamba-2; leave global attention.
10. **Gated DeltaNet 2** — same placement (local layers only).
11. **Kimi Linear** — same placement (local layers only).
12. **NSA** — native sparse attention.
13. **Over-encoding** — over-encoded input embeddings.

### Needs a spec/paper link (post-cutoff or under-specified for me)
14. **DeepSeek-V4 activation** on SwiGLU.
15. **DeepSeek-V4.1 attention design.**
16. **TST** — https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.06546 (post my knowledge cutoff; will fetch/confirm spec).
17. **Block attention residuals.**
18. **Engram.**
19. **Manifold / hyper-connections.**

Skipping (from the top-30 list): #4 differential attention, #5 attention sinks.

## Links
* fast_track PR: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9287
* Ablation study (feature removals): #9288

## Decision Log

## Conclusion

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 Resolved paper links / specs for the feature list (Kimi Linear = KDA confirmed):

**Attention / SSM**
- MLA — DeepSeek-V2, [arxiv 2405.04434](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.04434)
- Mamba-2 — [arxiv 2405.21060](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.21060)
- Gated DeltaNet (base) — [arxiv 2412.06464](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.06464); **Gated DeltaNet-2** (decouples erase/write; generalizes GDN + KDA) — [arxiv 2605.22791](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.22791)
- Kimi Linear / **KDA** (Gated DeltaNet + fine-grained per-channel diagonal gating; hybrid w/ MLA) — [arxiv 2510.26692](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.26692); ref impl: github.com/MoonshotAI (KDA)
- NSA — DeepSeek Native Sparse Attention, [arxiv 2502.11089](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.11089)
- DeepSeek-V4 attention (CSA = compressed-KV + sparse DSA; HCA = heavy-compression dense; interleaved) — [arxiv 2606.19348](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19348)
- DeepSeek-V4.1 attention (CSA2: per-layer Full/Reindex/Reuse KV sharing; two-tier 128-tok window + compressed-KV every ~6 layers; CED encoder-decoder) — no arxiv; [HF: deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash](https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash), [writeup](https://erogol.substack.com/p/deepseek-v41-flash-new-asymmetric)

**Residual / connections / norm**
- Block attention residuals — "Attention Residuals" (Kimi Team; learned depth-wise attention over layer outputs; Block-AttnRes groups ~8 blocks) — [arxiv 2603.15031](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.15031), github.com/MoonshotAI/Attention-Residuals
- Manifold / hyper-connections — DeepSeek-V4's **mHC (Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections)** in [2606.19348](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19348), built on **Hyper-Connections** [arxiv 2409.19606](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.19606)
- Sandwich norm (Gemma-2), logit soft-cap (Gemma-2), learnable residual gain (LayerScale), parallel attn+FFN (PaLM/GPT-J) — standard, no paper fetch needed

**FFN / embeddings / memory / training**
- DeepSeek-V4 activation — clamped SwiGLU (clamp gate/up to a swiglu_limit; low-cost, no exp/div), from [2606.19348](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19348)
- Over-encoding — "Over-Tokenized Transformer: Vocabulary is Worth Scaling" (large n-gram input vocab via tiled/decomposed embedding) — [arxiv 2501.16975](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.16975)
- MTP — DeepSeek-V3, [arxiv 2412.19437](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.19437)
- Tied embeddings — standard
- Engram — DeepSeek "Conditional Memory via Scalable Lookup" (hashed token n-gram O(1) lookup fused into residual via gating) — [arxiv 2601.07372](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.07372)
- **TST** — "Efficient Pre-Training with Token Superposition" [arxiv 2605.06546](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.06546) — NB: this is a **training method** (superposition phase w/ multi-hot CE, then recovery), *not* an architecture change; it wouldn't be a per-feature model branch but a training-loop change.

spillover_issues.author: dlwh
spillover_issues.body:
## Goal

Test the boundary operator from [arXiv 2609.19107](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19107) ("How Model Growth, Recursion, and Boundary Operators Influence Scaling Exponents") on the grug MoE block, at matched parameters and FLOPs, before building any of the paper's looping/growth machinery.

The operator (paper's Operator-1, K=1, no looping, no growth): split the layers into prelude/core/coda (as even as possible; remainders to core first, then coda). The core starts from `h₀ = 0`, so its entry state is `BO(0, e) = α·e` where `e` is the prelude's output; after the last core block, the coda's entry state is `BO(h, e) = rms_norm(h) + α·e`. One RMSNorm and two vector-adds; zero new parameters.

Why this first: the paper reports the operator alone (no recursion, no growth) already moves the scaling exponent — effective compute multiplier ≈1.25× at 1e20 FLOPs. It is the cheapest decisive test of whether the paper's axes transfer to the MoE template: if the operator doesn't move the grug isoflop curves, looping/growth almost certainly won't either.

## Plan

- Variant `experiments/grug/moe_boundary/` copied from `experiments/grug/moe/` (copy-first per the grug archive workflow). Boundary-off is byte-identical to the parent (regression-tested on logits).
- Phase 0 arms at the four May Recipe compute-optimal cells (d512/3.82e17, d768/2.81e18, d1024/1.16e19, d1280/3.46e19), v4-32 EP=1, with the README measurement conditions pinned (seq 4096, PKO on, long RoPE on, z-loss off, batch/steps from the README table).
- d512 runs both α ∈ {1.0, 0.707} ("alpha insurance"; paper's tuned values for Operator-1 and Loop-2). Winner by final macro loss proceeds.
- Gate 1: effective speedup > 1 at d512 and d768 vs the README baselines (3.5422 @ 433,986 tok/s; 3.2273 @ 294,726).
- Gate 2: d1024 + d1280, refit `loss(C) = 1.6 + A·C^−α̂`, projections must beat 2.534 @ 1e21 and 2.205 @ 1e23; fitted α̂ vs 0.0941 is secondary evidence.
- Cost: ≈45 v4-32 slice-hours for the full phase; ≈7–8 for gate 1 alone.

## Records

Runs land in W&B project `marin_moe`, group `moe-boundary`. Results and the go/no-go call get recorded here as each gate resolves.

Part of #4281.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Analysis — scope: research experiment, no PR yet**

This is a multi-cell training experiment (variant + four v4-32 isoflop cells, two go/no-go gates, W&B recording), not a self-contained code fix. The workflow reserves PRs for small self-contained changes; larger/experiment work gets a reviewed approach first. Below is the grounded implementation design for the *code scaffolding* (the variant); launching the runs and resolving the gates is operator work (`use-iris` / grug launchers), not part of a code PR.

**Where the operator slots in.** The MoE forward loop iterates blocks linearly at [`model.py` L685–707](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/7b63e0d0cefcb19282fd9cc7efb3c109cbfc4801/experiments/grug/moe/model.py#L685-L707). Operator-1 (K=1, no loop/growth) wraps that loop:
- Split `self.blocks` into prelude / core / coda — even split, remainders to core first then coda.
- Run prelude on `hidden`; save `e = hidden` (prelude output).
- Core entry state `BO(0, e) = α·e` (core starts from `h₀=0`), so feed `α·e` into the first core block.
- After the last core block, coda entry state `BO(h, e) = rms_norm(h) + α·e`.
- Coda runs normally, then `final_norm` / `final_gated_norm` as today.

**Zero new parameters.** The paper's single RMSNorm is the existing non-parametric [`rms_norm` free function (`model.py` L252)](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/7b63e0d0cefcb19282fd9cc7efb3c109cbfc4801/experiments/grug/moe/model.py#L252) — reuse it; do not add an `RMSNorm` module. The two adds are plain vector adds.

**Config knobs.** Add to `GrugModelConfig` ([`model.py` L95–133](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/7b63e0d0cefcb19282fd9cc7efb3c109cbfc4801/experiments/grug/moe/model.py#L95-L133)) a single `boundary_alpha: float | None = None`. `None` ⇒ boundary off ⇒ the forward path must be byte-identical to the parent (the "boundary-off" regression baseline the issue asks for). Set `0.707` (1/√2) or `1.0` to enable. Avoid a separate boolean + float pair (compound-state anti-pattern per AGENTS.md).

**Variant location.** Copy `experiments/grug/moe/` → `experiments/grug/moe_boundary/` (copy-first, per `change-grug` / grug archive workflow; the issue's own plan agrees). Keep edits local; no shared framework surface. Add a `docs/reports/grug-archive.md` entry (origin `moe`, purpose, status `active`, diff link from the CI diff comment).

**Test that earns its place.** One regression test: with `boundary_alpha=None`, logits are bitwise-equal to the parent `moe` model on a fixed seed/input (the issue's "byte-identical" claim). Optionally a shape/finiteness check with `boundary_alpha=0.707`. No tautological tests.

**Open questions before coding:**
1. Per-cell `num_layers` for d512/d768/d1024/d1280 come from the May Recipe README table — confirm the exact counts so the even prelude/core/coda split is well-defined (e.g. how a 6-layer cell splits: 2/2/2).
2. Confirm the split is by *block index* only (the attention long/short pattern at L688–690 stays keyed to absolute layer index `i`, unchanged by the operator).
3. Should `boundary_alpha` also thread through the HF config round-trip (`to_hf_config`/`from_hf_config`), or stay experiment-only? Recommend experiment-only until it proves out.

I can implement the variant + regression test as a scoped PR on request (code only; runs excluded). Want me to proceed with that, or adjust the design first?

Part of #4281.

🤖 **Phase 0 result: gate 1 FAILS at d512; debug ladder exhausted**

**Full d512 sweep** (Paloma macro loss / avg last-100-step tok/s):
